Love the cowboy vibe!”

“It’s hard to beat JHMR for big terrain. The sidecountry is incredible, and even inbounds you can feel like you’re in a ski movie. Great snow and amazing views.”

Getting to Jackson Hole is easier thanks to expanded nonstop service from 14 cities, including a new route from Boston. Skiers can also show their boarding pass for a complimentary afternoon lift ticket, subject to availability. And for planning purposes, note that Ikon and Mountain Collective passholders will again need lift reservations, with daily mountain capacity managed by the resort.

Deep powder, easy parking, and a down-to-earth mountain vibe that’s getting harder to find.

Tucked on the western side of the Tetons, Grand Targhee is the kind of place skiers whisper about when they want to share a great find without blowing the whole place up. With more than 2,600 skiable acres and a reputation for reliably deep snow, it delivers the goods without the crowds, complications, or high-gloss resort scene that have become standard elsewhere. “I have been skiing Targhee for 20 years,” shared one Targhee fan. “It’s a treasure that makes me feel I have gone 25 years back in time—laidback, friendly, and what skiing in the U.S. used to be.”

Teton storms regularly roll through, piling light, dry snow onto Targhee’s west-facing slopes. When the flakes fly, the mountain’s wide-open bowls, spacious groomers, and well-spaced trees are primed for everything from playful powder laps to full-on face shots. The terrain may not match the sheer scale or intensity of nearby Jackson Hole, but there’s plenty to keep adventurous skiers entertained, such as Pat’s Face and the triple-black glades off the Dreamcatcher chair. And with snow ranking among the resort’s strongest attributes in our survey, your odds of finding something soft to ski are a big part of the draw.

Then there’s the experience off the slopes—or, more accurately, the lack of fuss surrounding it. Parking is refreshingly manageable, the atmosphere is welcoming, and families can focus on skiing instead of navigating a complicated resort operation. Employees are genuinely friendly, locals are happy to share their favorite stashes, and nobody seems particularly interested in impressing anyone. Grand Targhee’s value is another major selling point: You’re here for the snow and the skiing, not for a designer village or a scene that requires a reservation.

The base area keeps things simple, with a handful of lodging and dining options and the ever-popular Trap Bar for post-ski beers and stories. For more restaurants, coffee shops, and après options, head down the road to Driggs, Idaho, a growing mountain town with plenty of independent character. Lodging and nightlife aren’t Targhee’s strongest suits, and anyone looking for a sprawling resort village may come away underwhelmed. But that’s also the point. This is a place where the mountain takes center stage, and the rest is refreshingly uncomplicated. “The vibe is quaint yet the slopes are expansive,” summed up one survey respondent.

“I loved the way the resort was laid out. It’s really easy to understand the trail map and navigate the various areas.”

Two enormous mountains, world-class alpine terrain, and a village that knows how to keep the party going.

Whistler Blackcomb is the kind of place that makes you want to extend your trip before the end of your first day. This sprawling British Columbia megaresort ranked No. 1 for terrain variety in our survey for good reason: Between the two mountains, skiers can spend days bouncing between wide-open alpine bowls, steep chutes, glades, glaciers, and cruisers that let you catch your breath before doing it all again. Whether you’re chasing technical lines or simply want to explore a mountain that seems to go on forever, Whistler delivers big-mountain skiing with an international flavor few resorts can match. “Loved the vastness of Whistler.,” said one survey respondent. “Went with a group; every level of skier was happy.”

That international spirit extends straight into the pedestrian village, where après turns into dinner, dinner turns into drinks, and so on. The restaurants, boutiques, bars, and hotels draw visitors from across the globe, creating an energy that’s hard to replicate at a more isolated ski area. Readers ranked Whistler No. 1 for après, dining, and lodging, confirming that the experience here is about much more than clocking vertical. When the lifts close, the fun is only getting started. As one reader put it: “Whistler has the best après out of any resort in North America, hands down.”

Whistler’s popularity means crowded slopes and long lift lines, particularly during peak periods, while high prices can make a ski vacation here a serious investment. Readers also called out grooming and on-mountain food as areas where the experience doesn’t always live up to the mountain’s reputation. With terrain this extensive, conditions can vary considerably across the resort, and the sheer number of visitors can make finding your own patch of quiet snow a challenge. Still, for many skiers, those are the trade-offs that come with skiing one of the world’s great mountain destinations.

Whistler Blackcomb’s appeal is the sheer range of experiences packed into one place. You can spend the morning exploring high-alpine terrain, refuel on a sunny patio, and finish the day swapping stories over cocktails without ever needing to get in a car. This year, readers nudged the resort up to No. 8, a reminder that the combination of serious skiing and a seriously good time remains tough to beat. Just bring your legs, your appetite, and a realistic budget.

“Grew up here. Keep trying to find other resorts, but I keep coming back.”

The new Showcase Chair, a fixed-grip quad replacing the Showcase T-Bar, makes for easier access to Blackcomb’s high-alpine terrain. Whistler Blackcomb is also investing in its on-mountain dining: Dusty’s brings back breakfast, while Pika’s at the Roundhouse gets a renovation that includes a new coffee bar and an elevated comfort-food menu. At Steeps Grill & Wine Bar on Whistler Mountain and Christine’s on Blackcomb, enhanced outdoor patios add lounge seating, fire pits, and more reasons to linger over lunch.

Big Sierra storms, more than 3,500 acres of wildly varied terrain, and a ski-town vibe that runs on pure stoke.

Mammoth Mountain embodies the best of California ski culture: a big mountain, big storms, and a laidback vibe that makes skiing here feel different than anywhere else in North America. Tucked into the eastern Sierra Nevada, Mammoth has steadily earned its place among the West’s most beloved ski destinations, thanks to more than 3,500 acres of terrain and a refreshingly unpretentious ambience.

The terrain is as varied as it is expansive. Cruise wide-open groomers, hunt for wind-buffed powder in the bowls, or point your tips down steep, technical pitches that demand your full attention. The lift network makes it possible to cover serious ground, and on those bluebird days after a big storm, the mountain can feel almost limitless. “Mammoth lives up to its name,” agreed one reader. “The place is HUGE.” Mammoth’s famously long season is another draw: When plenty of other resorts have called it quits, this mountain often still has plenty of skiing left.

Of course, those legendary storms come with a catch. Sierra weather can be wild, and high winds frequently put upper-mountain lifts on hold. Knowing where to go—and when to pivot—is part of the Mammoth learning curve. The upside is that when the wind finally settles and the upper mountain opens, the payoff can be spectacular.

Getting here requires some commitment. Mammoth sits more than 300 miles from Los Angeles, making it a haul for Southern California weekend warriors and a serious road trip for just about everyone else. But that distance helps preserve the mountain’s independent spirit. Down in Mammoth Lakes, the vibe is more practical than polished, with a mix of craft breweries, restaurants, and places to refuel after a day on the hill. It may not be the most picturesque ski town in the West, but it has the essentials.

Mammoth isn’t for skiers who need every detail of a vacation to run like clockwork. But for those willing to roll with it, the reward is a big, unapologetically Californian mountain with terrain for nearly every ability and a culture that needs no reminder that this sport is supposed to be fun. Keep the expectations flexible, bring your stoke, and Mammoth can deliver the kind of days that keep skiers coming back. “Just a great mountain with terrain options for every taste. Great SoCal vibe.”

“I’ve been skiing there for 10 years now and everytime I go up, I experience something new.  If you want steeps, they’ve got that. If you want long groomers, they have those. Beginner terrain, there are multiple areas on the mountain to choose from. With the way the wind blows at Mammoth, it may not have snowed in three or four days but the wind buff creates wonderful stashes of powder. Basically, If you aren’t having a great time skiing at Mammoth, you’re not trying.”

Silky corduroy, fall-line steeps, and a real Western ski town that knows a thing or two about doing winter right.

Sun Valley has been winning over skiers for generations, and it’s not about to start chasing anyone else’s idea of a great ski resort. A longtime fixture in SKI’s rankings, the Idaho classic climbs from No. 8 to No. 6 this year on the strength of what it has always done exceptionally well: fast, impeccably groomed skiing, an efficient lift network, and service that makes the whole experience feel effortless. From the moment you pull up to the storied Sun Valley Lodge to your first carve down a freshly groomed run on Bald Mountain, there’s a sense that someone here has thought of everything. Consider it old-school hospitality with very good skiing attached.

Baldy, as the locals call it, is the main event. Its sustained fall-line pitches are tailor-made for skiers who like to lay over big, satisfying turns on perfectly manicured corduroy. The grooming is among the best around, and modern lifts make it easy to rack up laps without wasting half the morning in line. Families and newer skiers can head to Dollar Mountain, where approachable terrain offers room to build confidence. The trade-off? Sun Valley doesn’t have the sprawling mix of terrain found at some larger Western resorts, and natural snowfall can be less reliable than at its snowier neighbors. But the mountain operations team has earned its reputation for making the most of what falls from the sky. “Excellent snowmaking and grooming,” opined one Sun Valley skier. “The resort maintained terrific conditions—far better than any other U.S. resort—despite the lack of snow this season.”

Just down the road, Ketchum delivers the sort of genuine mountain-town character that can be hard to find amid the condos and carefully curated villages of newer resorts. Locals and visitors mingle over après drinks at the mix of trendier bars and well-established watering holes. The airport in nearby Hailey makes getting here easier than you might expect, with service from four major airlines connecting the area to eight U.S. cities. It’s still a trip that takes some planning, but the payoff is a ski vacation with a distinctive sense of place. “Sun Valley is magical. The town of Ketchum is a perfect ski town,” said one reader.

“Sun Valley always provides an exceptional experience. Their snowmaking and grooming is impeccable, always. While there may not have been much snow out West this season, I consistently skied over 50k vertical days! The village, restaurants, and Ketchum as a whole is a skiers paradise!”

Sun Valley is replacing two lifts this winter: Lookout Express will be upgraded to a detachable six-person lift and the Christmas fixed-grip quad will become a high-speed quad. They also added 50 acres of glades on Bald Mountain.

Sun Valley has also earned a first-in-the-nation DarkSky certification, recognizing its commitment to protecting the naturally dark night skies that make this corner of Idaho special.

Finally, for ski-racing fans, the Audi FIS Ski World Cup Finals return to Bald Mountain on March 19–25, bringing the world’s best racers to one of the sport’s most storied American venues.

A mountain of epic proportions, a lift network built for maximum laps, and enough Lone Peak bragging rights to last all winter.

Big Sky may have relinquished its No. 1 crown, but dropping to No. 5 is hardly a fall from grace. This is still one of North America’s most impressive ski experiences, with a seemingly endless supply of terrain, wide-open spaces, and a lift network that makes getting around a whole lot easier than it used to be. In southwestern Montana, Big Sky does everything on a big scale—and largely delivers. “When it comes to terrain, infrastructure, snow quality and natural splendeur, Big Sky is the real deal!”

The headliner is Lone Peak, whose 11,166-foot summit serves up steep chutes, exposed lines, and big-mountain terrain. But you don’t have to be a send-it-all-the-time expert to appreciate the place. Intermediates can rack up miles on rolling groomers and wide-open trails, while beginners have room to find their feet without feeling swallowed by the mountain. With so much terrain spread across the resort, there’s always another zone to explore and another reason to come back.

Boyne Resorts has spent years making that sprawling playground easier to ski, and the results are hard to miss. Heated high-speed lifts, including the eight-person Madison 8, keep the laps coming, while the Lone Peak Tram delivers skiers to the summit in less than four minutes. The new-last-season Explorer Gondola is the latest upgrade, connecting Mountain Village and the upper mountain, making it easier to spend more time skiing. It hasn’t gone unnoticed: “Big Sky has spent an extensive amount of money on new lifts,” commented one SKI reader. “Trams, gondolas, six- and eight-person bubble heated seat chairs. By far the closest to the European experience.”

Of course, skiing at this scale comes with a price tag to match. Readers dinged Big Sky for expensive lodging, on-mountain dining, and add-on costs, including parking and the tram ride to Lone Peak. The village could also use a little more après-ski energy once the lifts stop spinning. Town Center, a couple of miles down the road, offers more options for dinner and drinks, but Big Sky isn’t exactly the place to book if your ideal ski vacation involves dancing until last call. Then again, when the mountain is this good, an early bedtime and first chair might be just what the body needs.

“I skied there for four days and can ski another 40 and never get bored. Endless double and triple black lines off Lone Peak.  More and better expert terrain than anywhere I have seen in the U.S., but also fabulous terrain variety.”

It’s the first full winter for the 10-person Explorer Gondola and Kircliff Observatory. The gondola connects the base village with the Lone Peak Tram, and Kercliff, located at 11,166 feet, delivers sweeping 360-views across three states and two national parks.

Nearly 550 inches of snow a year, terrain worthy of its cult following, and a refreshingly old-school approach to skiing.

Some ski resorts sell a lifestyle. Alta sells skiing—and lots of it. Heading into its 89th season, this Little Cottonwood Canyon classic has climbed from No. 6 to No. 4 in our rankings, a reminder that you don’t need a flashy village or a thrilling après lineup to win over skiers. Alta is unapologetically skier-centric, resolutely low-key, and gloriously uninterested in keeping up with the Joneses. “A true skiers’ paradise.”

The snow helps. A lot. Alta earned the top spot in our snow category, thanks to nearly 550 inches of famously light Utah powder in an average season. When a storm rolls through, the mountain’s bowls, chutes, and steep pitches deliver the kind of deep, floaty turns that can make even a seasoned skier feel like a convert. “It’s powder heaven,” says one cult of Alta member. “All the best skiing days of my life have been at Alta.” But unlike some hardcore-favorite mountains, Alta isn’t exclusively for experts. There’s plenty of intermediate terrain, too, even if the steep-and-deep stuff tends to hog the spotlight.

The experience feels refreshingly old-school, from the modest base village to the emphasis on skiing over spectacle. Lodging and dining are available right at the mountain, and the overall cost can compare favorably with flashier destination resorts, particularly if you value time on snow over a resort-town nightlife scene. Families who appreciate a simpler ski vacation may find plenty to love here, though the lack of non-skiing diversions and the mountain’s skiers-only policy mean Alta isn’t everyone’s cup of cocoa.

Getting there can be the rub. Little Cottonwood Canyon traffic is notoriously challenging on powder days, weekends, and holidays, and a storm can turn the trip uphill into an exercise in patience. Staying in one of Alta’s village lodges can spare you some of the daily commute, but for everyone else, an early start and a flexible attitude are wise. Of course, once you’re floating through fresh snow, the traffic-induced grumbling tends to fade. That’s the Alta effect: You swear you’ll never sit in that canyon traffic again, then wake up the next morning and do it all over again. “When I die, you can bury me at Alta.”

“The terrain is phenomenal, but it’s not for everybody. It’s definitely a vibe.”

The multiyear renovation and expansion of Albion Lodge is complete, including the new Albion Grill with expanded patio seating. There’s also more opportunity for women to build skills and confidence with an expanded lineup of women’s camps, clinics, and lessons, led by experienced female instructors.

World-class lifts, seriously good food, and big-mountain skiing just 45 minutes from Salt Lake City. No wonder skiers keep coming back.

Snowbasin has been a reader favorite for years, and they’re not letting up: The Wasatch resort holds steady at No. 3 for 2027. Just 45 minutes from Salt Lake City, Snowbasin delivers big-mountain skiing with an unusually smooth experience from the parking lot to the last chair. That combination of easy access and painless parking is no small feat in Utah.

What really sets Snowbasin apart, though, is how well it does just about everything. The lifts are fast, the grooming is dialed, the guest service is excellent, and the on-mountain dining is a cut above the rest. The grand lodges feel more like mountain retreats than places to grab a quick lunch, and the terrain offers something for just about every kind of skier. Cruise the wide-open groomers off the DeMoisy Express, or head for the bowls, steeps, and cornices around Needles Cirque when you’re ready to get your heart rate up. It’s a mountain that can keep a mixed-ability group happy without anyone feeling like they’re compromising.

That polished experience extends to the people behind it. Snowbasin consistently earns high marks for guest service, and its dining options deliver both variety and quality. In other words, the mountain knows that a great ski day involves more than vertical feet. You’ll find plenty of places to refuel in style, whether you’re settling in for a leisurely lunch or just warming up between laps. “Everything is sublime!” said one happy Snowbasin skier. “The bathrooms are top-tier and the food is scrumptious, great gluten-free options compared to other resorts.”

There is one notable trade-off: No lodging at the base means Snowbasin isn’t a true destination resort in the traditional sense. And if you’re looking for a lively après scene right outside the lifts, you’ll need to look elsewhere. Luckily, nearby Ogden offers a range of places to stay, eat, and unwind, while Salt Lake City puts even more options within reach.

The bigger challenge these days is that the secret is decidedly out. Snowbasin has become a popular alternative when Little Cottonwood Canyon closes. With the resort slated to host alpine racing at the 2034 Winter Olympics, that spotlight will only grow brighter. The upside for skiers? Continued investment in lifts, terrain, and infrastructure that should make an already excellent mountain even better. “They’ve invested heavily in the lift infrastructure—the new Becker lift this season was a tremendous improvement and makes getting over to Strawberry so easy,” shared one survey respondent.

“Even in a low-snow winter, Snowbasin shined with a great experience. Their staff is the best in the industry, and the amenities are unbeatable. If you’re stuck on groomed trails, there really isn’t a better place. But on a powder day, this place really performs.”

Big-mountain terrain, jaw-dropping scenery, and a ski trip that won’t break the bank. What’s not to love?

A jump from No. 15 to No. 2 is no small feat, but Lake Louise has plenty going for it. Start with the value: Thanks to the favorable Canadian dollar, your ski-trip budget goes further here. Then there’s the skiing. Set within the spectacular wilderness of Banff National Park, Lake Louise serves up 4,200 acres of terrain with a distinctly Canadian Rockies flavor. Fast, confidence-building groomers? Check. Steep, rugged lines on the backside? Absolutely. Wide-open bowls, tree skiing, and enough variety to keep even seasoned skiers exploring? You bet. The scenery is almost unfairly good, too. As one reader put it, “Fantastic steep and deep chute skiing. No lines and amazing snow. Can’t be beat.”

The resort’s latest terrain additions make an already sprawling mountain even easier to explore. New connections link key areas of the mountain, while expanded glades give intermediate and advanced skiers more options in the trees. Snowmaking improvements on Richardson’s Ridge should also help deliver more consistent conditions when Mother Nature needs a little backup.

All of that said, you won’t find slopeside lodging or much in the way of après at the ski area itself. For that, head to Banff, a lively mountain town about 35 miles away with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and places to stay. Free, regular shuttles connect the town to the resort, so a rental car isn’t a must. And while Lake Louise may not have the buzzy village scene of some destination resorts, that’s part of its appeal: You come here for the mountain, the wilderness, and the kind of big-skiing experience that still feels refreshingly unpretentious. As one aficionado summed it up: “Lake Louise is simply the greatest. Love the mountain. Love Banff.”

“Lots of snow this year. I had some amazing powder days at Louise. The back bowls are some of my favorite areas to ski as well as the West Bowl. Even on non powder days, I enjoyed cruising in the alpine on the frontside.”

The resort adds Grove Glade, a groomed green run linking Merlin’s directly to the new Richardson’s Ridge chairlift, while Pikaboo and Prunepicker improve connections between key zones. Expanded intermediate and advanced glades offer even more tree-skiing options.

The resort is also upgrading the Top of the World chairlift to improve loading capacity, speed, and reliability, and expanding snowmaking coverage on Richardson’s Ridge for more consistent conditions.

A high-alpine playground with naturally reliable snow, fast lifts, and jaw-dropping Canadian Rockies views. Now, for the first time, it’s North America’s favorite ski resort.

There’s a reason skiers keep coming back to Banff Sunshine. Actually, there are several: big-mountain scenery, reliably good snow, a long season, and terrain that ranges from mellow groomers to legitimately intimidating steeps. “High elevation means great quality and plentiful snow throughout the very long season,” wrote one Sunshine fan. “Always finding new fun spots even though I’ve been skiing here for years.”

And then there’s the setting. Just 15 minutes from the lively town of Banff, Sunshine feels like a world apart once you’re riding the gondola up through the trees toward its sprawling, above-treeline playground. It’s the kind of place that reminds you why you ski in the first place.

This year, our readers put Banff Sunshine at the top of North America’s 50 best resorts for the first time ever, bumping it up from last year’s No. 2 ranking. It makes sense. Sunshine has invested in its lift system in recent years, making it easier to explore the mountain and a whole lot more comfortable to ride on blustery days. Bubble enclosures on select lifts are a particularly welcome touch at a resort where exposed alpine terrain is part of the appeal—and where the weather can be as big as the views.

The skiing itself offers plenty of ways to spend a day. Cruise rolling groomers, roam across wide-open bowls, or work your way toward the steeper, more technical terrain. For experts, Delirium Dive is talked up a lot, but don’t overlook some other sleepers, including Stampede and Saddledome on Goat’s Eye Mountain. Sunshine may not have the sheer variety of some larger North American resorts, but its mix of approachable laps and high-alpine challenges makes it an easy place for a group with different abilities to enjoy skiing together.

Then there’s the snow. With a summit just shy of 9,000 feet and no snowmaking, Sunshine depends entirely on Mother Nature—and has the elevation and climate to make the most of it. Its season regularly stretches into late May, giving skiers a shot at spring turns long after many other resorts have called it a year. That extended season, combined with the big-mountain setting, is a pretty compelling argument for making the trip. “Banff is my favorite place to ski,” opined one survey respondent. “The mountain is beautiful, the terrain is varied, and it’s not overcrowded. The town of Banff is perfect. Like a postcard. Most beautiful place in North America.”

The one catch? You can’t exactly roll out of bed and onto the lifts from a sprawling slopeside resort village. Sunshine Mountain Lodge is the ski area’s only overnight accommodation, and scoring a room means waking up to a rare kind of quiet, with first tracks practically on your doorstep. Everyone else can stay in Banff, where free shuttles make getting to the mountain refreshingly simple. The town has everything from affordable hotels to more upscale digs, plus enough restaurants, bars, bowling alleys, and other diversions to fill an evening—or several. The combination of wild alpine skiing by day and a proper mountain town by night is hard to beat.

What’s New The ski area is amping up its après offerings this season. The GOAT Club returns to Goat’s Eye Lodge for a second season of live music, DJs, and après parties, and the new Coco Lounge, on the deck of the Centennial Lodge, will serve cocktails and food with fireside seating and slope views. If you need a warm-up between laps,  Coco Lab Coffee & Hot Chocolate Bar is now at Goat’s Eye Lodge serving hot drinks. There’s also a new cocktail bar if you want something a little stronger.

#8242. The Best Survival Food, Tested and Reviewed

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Regarding survival, a reliable food supply is high on the list of needs for disaster readiness. A well-rounded, easy-to-transport kit that keeps you nourished for days—without repeating the same bland meals—is crucial for morale and sustenance.

Many survival food companies are on the market, but not all have stood the test of time. Over the years, several have failed due to poor quality control and mismanagement. As a disaster readiness and survival training professional, I receive samples from many of these companies and, more importantly, have the unique opportunity to have hundreds of students test their products yearly. Additionally, I bring these samples to our courses to gather feedback from our instructors and participants. The insights shared in this article are based on decades of personal experience and the collective input of our students, providing you with a well-rounded perspective to help you make informed decisions about your food preparedness.

At the end of the day, no matter the crisis, we all need food to keep us going. While it’s true that humans can survive for weeks without eating, very few would willingly test that theory. The good news is that with the growing demand, more high-quality, nutrient-dense options are now available. After testing some of the best survival food on the market, these are our top picks for flavor, shelf life, and nutrition.

4Patriots has established itself as one of the leading survival food brands in the market. Proudly made and packaged in the United States, their products support local businesses while delivering high-quality meals. These meals are crafted for superior nutrition and taste, using fresh ingredients and whole grains, and are free from MSG. Preparation is simple—boil water, add the pouch, and within 15 minutes, you’ll have a hot meal ready to eat.

4Patriots packages their food in triple-layer Mylar to ensure long shelf life, which helps protect the contents from air and moisture. Customers can select from various kit sizes depending on their needs, from 72-hour emergency supplies to year-long provisions. Each kit is designed to provide one person with six servings a day, offering sufficient calories and nutrients to sustain energy. The meals come in various flavors, including macaroni and cheese, vegetable soup, and oatmeal. One of my favorite pieces of their kits is that many of the meals are named after people to add some morale build into it all.  No matter the kit size, 4Patriots offers a reliable solution for building a robust survival food supply.

A vital feature of an MRE is the built-in heater, which, once activated, heats your entrée, providing the convenience of a hot meal no matter where you are. However, there are some notable downsides. Many of our students, particularly those with military experience who have relied on MREs for extended periods, advise against using them for long-term situations. In addition to being heavy to transport, they can lead to digestive problems, ranging from constipation to more organ-related severe issues over time.

Providing a hot meal for your family during a disaster is more than just a practical necessity—it can help boost morale and alleviate anxiety, offering a sense of normalcy amidst the chaos. Mountain House meals taste delicious and require boiling water for preparation. Mountain House is a regular staple of meal choices in our classes. I see them often.

One of the great features is that the food rehydrates directly in the pouch, allowing you to eat from it, which means minimal cleanup afterward. With nearly 30 meal options, including breakfasts and desserts, variety won’t be an issue, and no one will find the meals repetitive.

Each serving offers about 250 calories, depending on the meal. With two servings per pouch, there’s plenty for even a hearty appetite or enough to share if needed. These meals are designed to stay fresh for up to 30 years and ensure you can access quality food for decades.

Crafted with Whey Protein Isolate as the primary protein source and fortified with high fiber while containing just 1 gram of sugar, these protein bars are perfect for daily enjoyment. Each Kirkland Signature bar offers 21 grams of high-quality protein and features real chocolate for a satisfying blend of taste and nutrition. Typically used for meal replacement and workout-focused diets, these bars conveniently meet your protein and fiber needs without compromising flavor.

In the context of disaster preparedness, these protein bars are an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Their long shelf life, combined with their nutritional profile, makes them an excellent option for staying energized and nourished when fresh food may not be available. Lightweight and easy to store, they offer a reliable source of protein and fiber that can help maintain energy levels and support overall health during a crisis. Whether sheltering in place or on the move, these bars ensure access to essential nutrients in challenging circumstances.

Augason Farms is renowned for its extensive line of canned goods, which are perfect for long-term food storage and emergency preparedness. Their #10 cans are filled with freeze-dried or dehydrated foods, offering various essentials, such as fruits, vegetables, meats, grains, and dairy products. With a shelf life of up to 25 years, these canned goods are an excellent choice for those looking to build a reliable food supply for emergencies or everyday convenience. Each can is sealed for freshness and labeled with detailed preparation instructions, making incorporating these products into daily meals or survival situations easy.

Augason Farms’ canned goods are appealing because of their versatility and nutritional value. Whether you need individual ingredients like powdered eggs, instant potatoes, or freeze-dried strawberries, their products allow for flexibility in meal planning. You can use them in recipes or enjoy them independently, ensuring you have access to nutritious food options when fresh ingredients are unavailable. These canned goods are compact, easy to store, and offer large quantities, making them ideal for families, survivalists, or anyone seeking to stock up on essential food supplies that can withstand the test of time.

Peak Refuel is a top choice for disaster preparedness, offering high-protein, freeze-dried meals designed to keep you fueled during challenging situations. Maintaining strength and energy is essential in emergencies, and Peak Refuel meals deliver an impressive 40-50 grams of protein per serving. This high protein content ensures you get the nutrition needed to stay alert and physically capable when it matters most. Whether you’re sheltering in place or need to be on the move, these meals provide the sustenance required to get through physically demanding conditions.

Beyond their nutritional value, Peak Refuel meals are incredibly convenient for disaster preparedness. Made with high-quality, non-GMO ingredients, they rehydrate quickly with hot water and are ready to eat in minutes. The lightweight, resealable pouches are easy to store and transport, making them an ideal addition to any emergency food supply. Various meal options, including breakfast scrambles and hearty dinners like chicken alfredo or beef stroganoff, offer the nutrients you need and great taste to keep morale high during tough times. Peak Refuel’s focus on protein-rich, easy-to-prepare meals makes them an excellent choice for anyone serious about disaster readiness.

ReadyWise is a leading provider of long-term food storage solutions, offering various affordable, high-quality meals that are perfect for disaster preparedness. Whether you’re planning for a short-term emergency or looking to build a comprehensive survival food stockpile, ReadyWise provides convenient, easy-to-prepare options. Their freeze-dried meals only require water, making them ideal for emergencies or outdoor adventures where resources may be limited. With a focus on both taste and nutrition, ReadyWise ensures that their products not only sustain you during a crisis but also offer flavors you can enjoy.

One of the standout features of ReadyWise is its budget-friendly approach, making it a top choice for those who want to prepare without breaking the bank. Despite the lower price point, ReadyWise doesn’t compromise on quality or variety, offering satisfying and nutritionally balanced meals. This combination of affordability and convenience makes ReadyWise a smart investment for families and individuals looking to secure a reliable food supply for potential emergencies. With ReadyWise, you can build your preparedness plan without overspending, ensuring peace of mind for whatever the future holds.

To select the foods we tested, we received samples from a variety of reputable companies and also purchased additional products to ensure a wide range of options. With the help of our students, who have diverse tastes and preferences, we got a broad spectrum of feedback during the testing process. These foods were integrated directly into our survival and disaster readiness training courses, allowing us to evaluate their practicality, taste, and ease of preparation in real-world scenarios. This hands-on approach ensured that we tested the food’s quality and performance under survival conditions.

A structured approach to survival prioritization is best understood through the “Law of Threes” hierarchy. This principle outlines that our most immediate needs, in order of importance, are safety, thermoregulation, hydration, and finally, food. However, from a psychological and moral standpoint, food remains a constant desire, even though it ranks lower on essential needs.

We also took a multi-tiered approach to assessing these survival food options.  I am fond of saying that “hunger is the best seasoning in the world.”  That is true in the long term, but taste plays a role in the short term.  When assessing them, I emphasize both taste and cost-effectiveness. After all, it makes little sense to invest in provisions that are not enjoyable to eat. In addition to these factors, I consider the following critical criteria in my recommendations:

One of the most overlooked factors when choosing survival food is whether or not you enjoy eating it. Taste, texture, and how the food agrees with your digestive system are essential. While it’s easy to focus on stockpiling a large quantity of food, if you don’t like it, you’re essentially wasting money. Some may argue that you’ll eat anything in extreme hunger, but right now, you have the luxury of selecting food you’ll enjoy. Regularly incorporating these meals into your current diet helps rotate stock and prepares your taste buds for when disaster strikes. As the saying goes, “We do not rise to the occasion; we default to our level of training.” Why not start training your palate now?

Cost is another critical consideration when building a survival food supply. Most people must budget carefully, so simultaneously making large purchases may be impossible. A gradual approach works well for many, where small amounts are bought over time as the budget allows. This makes the process more manageable and helps you steadily grow your stockpile without straining your finances. If you face resistance from family members about spending on survival food, consider framing it as an insurance policy—something you invest in for peace of mind in case of a worst-case scenario.

Storage space can be a real challenge for those living in smaller spaces like apartments, condos, or tiny homes. It’s crucial to make the most of your space by considering the size of the packaging and the number of servings per product. This ensures you get the most food stored in the least space. Carefully evaluating your storage setup and choosing compact, efficient products can help maximize your shelf space and investment.

Storing survival food is best done in conditions that are dark, cool, and dry. These three factors will work together to slow down the degradation of the food. A closet in a spare bedroom, for example, might be a great location. A damp basement, perhaps not so much.

Most survival situations tend to last around 72 hours. However, in recent years, many emergencies have extended beyond that timeframe, and with global uncertainty, the possibility of more prolonged events is not just possible but increasingly likely. As a precaution, I recommend planning for at least one month’s worth of food for everyone in your household, ensuring you’re prepared for longer-term scenarios.

As previously mentioned, our primary needs follow a specific order: safety, thermoregulation, water, and food. For safety, ensure you have the tools necessary to protect yourself from both environmental threats and potential harm from others. This includes items to help you see in low-light situations and defend yourself if needed. Thermoregulation involves staying warm in cold weather and cool in hot conditions, so be sure to have adequate clothing and supplies to maintain comfort for at least one month without access to utilities.Water is an invaluable resource, and it’s crucial to have both filtration and purification methods to protect against bacterial and viral contaminants. In addition to these essentials, it’s wise to have signaling tools like bright-colored items, flashlights, and whistles to help attract attention if necessary.

Choosing survival food to keep on hand for emergencies requires a little homework and research. You shouldn’t buy several cases of something simply because the package looks enticing. Base your decision on facts, including budget and the quality of the food. Ease of preparation is also a factor, of course. In an emergency, you may not have ready access to things like stovetops or microwave ovens. Stick with things that require a minimal amount of preparation. Hopefully, you’ll never be in a situation where you must rely on survival food, but you’ll be glad you have it should the unthinkable occur.

Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. #8241. The Best Ski Packs of 2027, Tested in the Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Our 14 testers ran 18 packs through a season of fast transitions, steep bootpacks, and long days to find the best of 2027. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: The best backcountry ski packs of 2027 include the Ortovox Venet 30 ($170) for most skiers, the Raide EX55 ($599) for expeditions, the Dynafit Radical 30 Snow Pack ($190), and the Rab Descendor 40 Ski Pack ($200) for ski mountaineering. Our 14 testers—men and women—evaluated 18 packs over a full season in Colorado, Utah, Alaska, the Alps, and more, judging fit, weight distribution, access, and durability.

When traveling in the backcountry, it’s not just what you bring but how you carry it. Intuitive access points make finding and stashing items easy, and externally fastened gear needs to stay secure without blocking pockets. But making the most of capacity is arguably the most critical feature. As our testers make tracks farther out in the mountains and become more self-reliant, they tend to reach for higher-volume packs that can fit everything they need without overloading them to the point of a skin track gear explosion. We factored comfort into all of it while testing 18 packs, narrowing the field to the best backcountry ski packs of 2027 for every type of ski adventure.

Pros and Cons + Triple-zipper access + Huge hipbelt pocket – A-frame carry blocks pack access and the diagonal carry strap was a little tricky to access

Ski packs work best when you can avoid taking them all the way off and rooting through the main compartment when you need to pull out gear. That means shorter stops in the skin track—if you stop at all—which helps you keep momentum and body temperature up on cold days. The Venet 30 features triple-zipper access to the main compartment, which let our tester quickly grab his water flask while skinning around Hemavan, Sweden, and Helgeland, Norway. The large hipbelt was also a tester favorite. “While I loved the elastic waist on the Ortovox Freerider, the normal hip strap with the pocket on the Venet was a huge plus for general touring,” said one. “On longer days I kept snacks in it and on more freeride days I kept a GoPro, for which easy access allowed me to actually remember to pull my cam out before descents.”

Testers called this the most ergonomic and versatile pack they’ve used from Ortovox, thanks to its simplicity, the comfortable adjustability of its straps, and its full-contact back panel. The mini top pocket was well sized—not too deep and easy to access—and the hidden mini pocket in the avalanche tool compartment was useful for carrying an emergency bivy and small med kit, keeping them “out of the way” of the rest of your gear.

This pack’s ideal use is general touring with the occasional bootpack, but it’s capable as a more technical bag when ropes may be required. It performs well as a freeride sidecountry bag or on longer tours—comfortable for mellow days and functional for technical ones.

Features that would make this pack even more user-friendly: a small zip on the right back side to mirror the bottom zipper for water access, the ability to carry two ice axes (the elastic cord holds only one), and easier access to the pack when using side ski-carry.

Pros and Cons + Modular volume + Rolltop closure – No external helmet carry

Schlepping all your gear on a big hut trip or expedition-style endeavor has long presented a dilemma: how to carry a pack big enough for everything at basecamp while also having a daypack small enough for lighter missions. Bringing two packs is inefficient, but skiing with a few items jiggling loose in a giant frame pack feels cumbersome. The Raide EX55 expands to 75L and carries enormous loads, then cinches down once you’ve emptied most items out, so it skis like a little daypack. “During our big four-day ski traverse out of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, I’d get to the base of a couloir, fill a bivy sack with all our junk, cinch the pack down, and boot up like I had a regular ski pack on,” said our Mammoth-based tester. “It skis incredibly well given how much gear it can swallow.”

Raide accounts for the added weight with thicker shoulder and hip straps and better load lifters than its smaller counterparts, the LF30 and LF40. All of it is ideal for heavier hauls. The EX55 doesn’t just turn into a giant sack and skimp on key features. You can still deploy your probe without taking off your pack—ideal for glacier travel of any kind—and the same goes for the shovel with the pack on one shoulder. Testers called the ski carry systems excellent, and being able to grab an ice tool without removing the pack is invaluable in steep bootpacks. “This pack strips backcountry skiing down to its absolute essentials but lets you do it on a bigger scale,” said one.

The one complaint we heard was that the EX55 lacks the external drop sleeve found in the LF30 and LF40 for carrying helmets and skins, so when the pack is loaded for overnight carries, it’s tough to stuff skins in and out of the front zip pocket. It also makes the pack very tall when fully loaded with a helmet inside.

Weight: 2.31 lbs Size: Women’s, Universal

Pros and Cons + Thick back panel padding + Easy-access diagonal-carry bungee cord strap – Not ideal for those who pack extra gear

When you’re banging out hot laps, your pack should feel like part of your body. This one holds tight to smaller female torsos and disappeared on the back of another Sierra tester last spring as she skied 1,500- to 7,000-foot days on Mount Shasta, in the Eastern Sierra and at Lake Tahoe’s Rubicon Peak. “This pack skied really well, and gear that’s good enough to disappear is my favorite,” she said  after testing other packs with hipbelts that didn’t curve as ergonomically as this one.

Testers appreciated the top, rear-panel, and side zips, which made it easy to organize their stuff inside and keep things like crampons and water readily accessible. The avy gear gets its own pocket with a wide zipper, and an ice axe can be removed without taking the pack off, as can skis with a skimo-style diagonal carry bungee strap.

At 30 liters, it’s right on the edge of fitting everything you might want to carry on a day tour. “When I went out to the Norman Clyde Couloir, conditions were cold and windy, so I wanted to carry more than I usually do for a day tour,” said our tester. “The pack fit snacks, 1 liter of water, a hardshell, a puffy, ski and boot crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a slender rescue sled, avy gear, a small first aid kit, and two pairs of gloves. I was definitely worried about busting the zipper, but it held all day.” The load lifters worked well to support this weight, and the thick back panel kept hard items like water bottles from poking into her back. If you prefer to bring this much stuff or more on most outings, you may find this pack a little too small.

Pros and Cons + Spot-on fit + Long side zipper accesses items of any size – Wobbly elastic diagonal ski carry

Spring ski mountaineering missions can mean longer days, longer approaches, and extra gear—crampons, more water, sometimes ropes—so you need a pack that carries it all in an efficient, functional arrangement. Loading it up is one thing; accessing it is another. The Descendor 40 balances both with a few key features. Our Colorado-based tester was a big fan of the side-access zipper, which is functionally useless if it isn’t long enough. This one is plenty long, and it was the only access point he needed while touring. He could easily pull out anything inside, including a large DSLR camera, skins, and a food bag, and he opened the rolltop closure only during full transitions.

The pack also has the best integration of hydration features. “On the right strap, there is a perfect pocket to carry a soft flask, including a strap to secure the flask against jostling,” our tester said. “I have lost soft flasks while skiing in other packs and am not worried about that on this pack. On the left shoulder strap, there is a small zippered pocket that is an appropriate size to carry items like gels, sunscreen, lip balm, etc. Overall, these features made it easy to stay hydrated and sunscreened on a fast and light ski tour.”

Testers lauded the comfortable back panel, wide hip straps, padded shoulder straps, and load lifters when needed. The pack carries weight well and fits true to size.

This pack is designed for long, efficient ski tours and glaciated summit pushes where ropes and technical gear are needed. It has features for ski mountaineering and carries additional gear like ice tools, with a gear loop for carabiners and a system for quickly strapping skis to the pack. The rolltop is an attempt to make the pack more versatile—a 40L pack that can act as a 25L—but it needs some refinement to better accommodate smaller volumes. Our tester also found the elastic strap for diagonal ski carry too long, and his skis bounced around while bootpacking couloirs.

Built for fast pow laps and and slackcountry days, the Dakine Heli 2.0 is everything you need to stay well equipped on your next mountain adventure. From diagonal ski and splitboard carry to vertical or horizontal snowboard carry, it doesn’t matter your style—it can get your gear wherever you need to go. The pack’s fleece-lined pockets keep your goggles smudge-free, and the snow tool sleeves keep your smaller items organized and accessible. And maybe most importantly, RECCO Technology helps keep you searchable in case of an avalanche or rescue.

Weight: 2.1 lbs (35L, S/M) Sizes: S/M, M/L

Pros and Cons + Easy access to inside storage + Removable snowboard carry straps – Avalanche tool pocket is too large

It’s a bold move to update a classic product, but Black Diamond took a leap on the tried-and-true Cirque by making several big changes. The brand added a side zipper to access the main compartment and more durable materials, including a PFC-free 210D nylon fabric and Dynex grid that’s stronger than the older version and more water repellent. Testers loved these new features and didn’t encounter any durability issues during the whole season of slamming the pack on and off in quick transitions with sharp ski edges and tools rubbing on the outside.

The new Cirque 35 excels on spring missions in the alpine, where quick access to crampons, an ice axe, and other gear is key. “I love a roll-top pack, and this is one feature that I really appreciate,” says one tester who toured it during winter and spring days around Aspen, Colorado. “I was able to throw in an extra layer for tours without hesitation because of the space it offered and how easy it was to get in and out, especially with the large side zipper.” The diagonal ski carry system with a bottom loop and top webbing strap with a hook was quick and easy to deploy in transition, and the ice-axe bungees were a breeze to unfasten on unexpected sections of steep terrain.

Our 6’1″ tester thought the pack was a bit short, and some disliked the hassle of opening both the webbing hook and roll-top buckle to get inside. Snowboard straps are sturdy but removable when you don’t need to carry a board on your pack.

Pros and Cons + Excellent freedom of movement + Compact fit – Limited carrying capacity

Skiing or snowboarding with too much extra space in a backpack allows the contents to rattle around inside, which can be an annoying distraction. Our Montana tester didn’t have that problem when hiking the ridge at Bridger Bowl, their local ski resort, with this compact, 15-liter pack with clever pocket placement and internal organization. Thanks to the low profile, it was comfortable enough to wear on the chairlift, and the fit felt snug while riding, too, with padding in all the right spots on the upper back, hips, and shoulder straps.

“It didn’t flop around at all like bigger packs do when empty, nor did it limit my movement in bumps or when really laying down carves,” another Montana tester said after securing the pack’s wide, sturdy hipbelt. They rode with this pack at Bridger Bowl in sub-freezing temperatures, requiring extra fuel and layers, and didn’t feel that it was too bulky. He also appreciated the glove-friendly A-frame and vertical ski carry options on short sidecountry hikes and bootpacks, along with snowboard straps and an internal avalanche tool compartment for sidecountry missions.

Overall, this is a small, space-efficient pack with smart pockets (fleece-lined goggle and external side zip) for short missions just beyond the gates or for fully-supplied resort laps.

Packs come in various sizes to fit different torso lengths, so measure your spine from the base of your neck to the top of your hips and choose your size accordingly. Torso lengths generally range from 15 inches, or size XS, to 20-plus inches, or size L. Because fit is the single most significant factor in pack comfort and carry, we recommend going to your local gear shop wearing the layers you plan to tour in and trying packs on. The hipbelt should securely wrap your iliac crest, and the back panel shouldn’t hit the back of your head when you’re wearing a helmet.

If half-day backcountry tours are your norm, choose a lower-volume pack, 20 to 30 liters, that fits just the essentials—shovel, probe, water, extra layers, snacks. If you typically spend full days in the backcountry, you’ll want a higher-volume pack, 30 to 40 liters, with room for the extra supplies you’ll need out in the elements. For overnight trips and expeditions, look for a 50-plus-liter pack.

Also make sure your avalanche shovel and probe slip easily in and out of the dedicated avy pouch in an emergency, and that the pack is big enough and organized enough for how you tour. Don’t be afraid to size up if you’re unsure how much space you’ll need—a few extra liters of empty space won’t weigh you down much. If you want to secure your skis to your pack, look for an A-frame or diagonal ski-carry strap system and back-panel suspension that can support the extra weight. The same goes for your helmet: most packs have integrated helmet carry, but not all do, so double-check if it’s essential to you.

Always carry avalanche safety equipment when traveling in the backcountry. That means wearing a beacon and carrying a shovel and probe in your pack. You’ll also need extra layers, a helmet, sufficient hydration—including something hot in an insulated bottle on longer backcountry days—snacks, a first-aid kit, and a basic repair kit.

To nail down the best ski packs of 2027, we seeded 18 products with 14 different testers. Each tester was matched to packs according to their planned objectives, body type, ability level, and testing environments. Then we set testers loose in the mountains, mainly in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Washington, California, and Alaska, with a few trips to Scandinavia and the Alps. Testers jammed gear into packs, stuffed them shut, and pushed them to their limits on both rugged and mellow ski ascents and descents.

We focused on newly designed packs with practical, ski-specific features that make traveling on snow easier, safer, and more enjoyable. We also brought tried-and-true, unchanged models into the mix so you’re seeing the best of what’s available. Comfort is a must, even for packs meant to carry smaller, lighter loads, as is durability, so we asked testers to evaluate straps, back panels, and hipbelt carry alongside the quality of materials.

Every time a pack went out, testers filled out feedback forms assessing fit, weight distribution, ease of access, and even pocket size and placement. Testers noted how easy it was to find what they needed, transition in the skin track, and carry their skis and boards on their backs while climbing steep couloirs. After a full season of rigorous testing, we selected the cream of the crop and reviewed those packs here.

Scott Yorko is a former gear editor for Backpacker, SKI, TransWorld SNOWboarding, and Outside. He lives in Colorado, where he splits his ski time between the world-class resorts around Aspen and the backcountry terrain of the West Elk Mountains. He loves to chase storms and visit pow-shredding friends, many of whom tested this year’s crop of ski packs in places like Alaska, Jackson Hole, the Sierra, Utah, and the Colorado Rockies.

#8240. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Early into the second night of the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

“I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He said, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

“We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll said. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was big: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

“I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”

Yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle says he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”

#8239. Why I’d Rather Take a Buck in the Timber

IT WAS LIKE the buck fell from the sky. I’d glassed the wooded creekbottom to my left only minutes before. Then I scanned the opposite timber, stared at my boots for a few seconds, and heard the slightest scuff in the leaves. Or I thought I did. This was my third straight morning in the stand, the point at which I can begin to hear phantom, wishful-thinking noises. But when I turned to look in the direction of the sound, there stood the buck, just 25 yards off, his hooves planted in a scrape.

I wasn’t nervous at first. In profile, his tines looked OK but not towering, and his ears were hiding whatever mass was there. But then he arched his neck to reach for the licking branch, and I caught my breath. Suddenly I could see his jumble of stickers and wrist-thick bases. I reached for my bow while he worked the scrape. Then, backing off the sign, he stood at the junction of two trails, where I could see the full depth of his chest and size of his flank. Either trail would bring him to a shooting lane 20 yards off my setup. He chose the one on the right, and when I touched off the shot, he made a 30-yard sprint, stopped, and tipped over dead.

The buck’s rack was in my top five at the time, and his body still ranks as my biggest. But what sticks with me most about that Kansas buck is how the hunt went down. I’d walked into an unknown piece of timber, walked it for 30 minutes, analyzing rubs, scrapes, trails, and topography, and then finally picked a stand tree, thinking, This is the spot where I can kill a nice buck. That doesn’t always work, of course, but when it does, it’s about as close to the perfect deer-hunting experience as I can imagine.

That may seem a little strange in today’s food-plot era—a time when more and more hunters hope to ambush deer out in the open and when we pore over which seeds to sow and even over the “architecture” and “design” of our elaborate ambushes. Don’t get me wrong. I’m a dedicated food-plotter. In 2009, I arrowed the biggest buck of my life, a heavy-beamed giant that grossed more than 180 inches, in a plot I’d helped plant just a month prior. Every year, I put in plots to hold deer through the season, to keep them fed in winter, for better shed hunting in spring, and for trail-cam monitoring in summer. But when it comes to actually tagging a buck, I would much rather do it in the timber.

I think the reason is simple but often overlooked these days. A buck feeding in a food plot is plain to see and a sight to behold—but still just a buck in a food plot. There’s not much to figure out there. But a buck bedded in the timber or side-hilling along a faint trail on the far side of a wooded ridge is a mystery. If you want to see this buck, you have to solve a puzzle, and to me, that’s the real fun of deer hunting.

Related: Want more whitetail stories? Sign up for the free Whitetail 365 Newsletter here.

It’s also the challenge. Anyone can plant turnips in the hope of luring deer to a chosen spot. The best hunters I know can walk the deer’s turf—the places where they hide and feel safe and call home—and, after a little snooping around, tell you exactly where you can kill a monster. Years back, I was scouting with my buddy Bob, who has a wall full of whopper bucks that speak to his deep understanding of mature deer. I was covering ground as quickly and thoroughly as my legs would allow. But nearly every time I looked at Bob, he was just standing there, scanning the terrain. Finally Bob gestured to a slight crease on an otherwise steep hillside. “What’s up there?” he asked.

“Well, it’s like a mini-bench, but I’ve walked it a bunch and never found a scrape or rub,” I told him.

“Doesn’t matter,” Bob said. “When I scout a place like this, the first thing I do is just stop and look. Then I imagine I’m pouring a big bucket of water on a hillside like that. And whatever contours the water would follow, that’s where the bucks will walk. If the sign is there, fine. But you don’t need it to know. You can kill a buck on that little bench, guaranteed.”

That day completely changed how I scout for deer. I’m excited to find a thigh-thick rub or a scrape that looks like an elk wallow, but mostly I study terrain. It’s a skill that I think can never be completely mastered, but occasionally I am able to decipher why a buck will move through this funnel and not that one, or how three ravines separated by hundreds of yards will work together to make one fence crossing the most incredible stand site ever.

Which brings me to the other simple reason to love hunting the timber. When a buck shows up at your food plot, it’s usually somewhat expected. After all, you’ve set the whole thing up for that purpose and probably have trail-cam pics or have glassed him there before. But when a buck shows up under your stand in the timber, it’s almost always a surprise.

Related: Red Oak vs White Oak, a Complete Guide for Hunters

A few Novembers back, while F&S executive editor Dave Hurteau and I readied for a morning hunt here in Minnesota, I told him I was going to try a hang-and-hunt in a new spot. “I’ve just got this place in my head,” I said. “I scouted it last spring, and there was almost zero buck sign. But it felt right.”

I’d picked the tree during my spring scouting mission, and I somehow found it in the dark that morning. Three climbing sticks and a tree step had me at stand height, and I hung the set and settled in. The first 90 minutes after a November sunrise are typically magic, but I wasn’t surprised when I saw exactly zero deer. The reason the small oak hollow had stuck with me was that it funneled toward bedding cover immediately behind me. But the deer heading there were starting from corn and soybean and alfalfa fields on farms over a half mile away. It was going to take some time for them to reach me.

Still, when I looked at my watch at 10:25, I was starting to doubt my hunch. Four deerless hours at the peak of the rut typically add up to Sorry bud, you guessed wrong today. But then I looked up and saw this perfect 10-point rack weaving through the timber. He stopped at just 10 yards before my arrow slipped through him. He wasn’t one of my biggest or heaviest, but I’d never seen the buck before, on camera or otherwise, which made him a perfect surprise and a puzzle solved, as unexpectedly as a Kansas deer falling from the sky.
