#8238. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8236. Vail Has Free On-Mountain Grills— Here’s Where to Find Them

Skiing isn’t exactly a budget-friendly sport. Between lift tickets, equipment rentals, and overpriced on-mountain meals, the costs can add up quickly. But tucked away at one of Colorado’s most famous ski resorts is an unexpected way to save money on lunch. Instead of spending a small fortune at an on-mountain restaurant, skiers can bring their own meats and grill them slopeside.

My husband and I have done exactly that; we packed our own meat for a midday cookout between runs at Vail Ski Resort. It’s one of those experiences that feels almost too good to be true, especially at a resort where even a casual lunch comes with a price.

And while saving money is certainly part of the appeal, there’s something special about taking a break from skiing to grill your own lunch surrounded by the Rocky Mountains.

Located in Blue Sky Basin, Belle’s Camp offers a different kind of dining experience. Rather than ordering from a menu, guests can bring their own food and use the public grills to prepare lunch.

“Belle’s Camp is meant to be a different kind of on-mountain dining experience,” says Kevin Delonay, Vail Mountain’s senior director of food and beverage. “Guests bring their own food, gather with friends and family, and make lunch part of their day in Blue Sky Basin.”

It’s a surprisingly simple concept. Pack whatever you’d like to eat, carry it with you while skiing, and head to Belle’s Camp when you’re ready for lunch. Burgers, hot dogs, and steaks are all possibilities, although you’ll want to consider how easily your food can be transported in a backpack.

Visitors should also pack whatever they need to enjoy their meal, including any necessary utensils, condiments, and other supplies. Since you’re carrying everything onto the mountain, keeping things simple can make the experience much easier.

The grills are available during Belle’s Camp operating hours when Blue Sky Basin is open, although availability is subject to mountain operations and weather conditions.

“There are plenty of places at Vail where we cook the meal for you,” Delonay says. “Belle’s is special because we provide the setting and guests create the experience themselves.”

One of the biggest advantages of grilling your own lunch is the potential savings, especially for families or groups skiing together.

At Vail, a typical on-mountain cafeteria lunch can cost around $20 per person, while a more upscale dining experience can cost considerably more. At The 10th, Vail’s full-service restaurant at the top of Gondola One, a Wagyu cheeseburger is listed at $45. For a family of four, a lunch on the mountain could add up to $80 to $180 before drinks or other extras.

Keep reading: Everything You Need To Know About The Hottest New Ski Lunch Trend

Instead, visitors can stop at a grocery store before their ski day and stock up on ingredients for a fraction of the cost. For example, a pack of hot dogs, buns, and a few toppings could feed several people for around $15 to $20. Burgers are another relatively inexpensive option, while those looking to make lunch more of an occasion can bring steaks.

Of course, the exact savings depend on what you purchase and how many people are in your group. But for families or friends already spending hundreds of dollars on lift tickets, rentals, and other ski expenses, packing lunch is one of the easiest ways to cut costs.

And unlike eating a cold sandwich on a chairlift, grilling your own meal gives you a chance to sit down, relax, and enjoy a warm meal on the mountain with a new sense of appreciation.

Despite being one of the resort’s more unusual experiences, Belle’s Camp isn’t necessarily something every first-time visitor knows about.

According to Delonay, much of its popularity has developed organically, with skiers introducing their friends and family to the experience.

“Belle’s Camp has really grown through word of mouth, and I think that’s part of its charm,” he says. “People discover it, bring their friends back and start their own traditions.”

That’s part of what makes the experience so memorable. Some visitors might stop for a quick burger between runs, while others turn lunch into a full-blown gathering with friends.

“We see everything from a simple lunch with friends to groups that really turn it into an occasion,” Delonay says. “That creativity is part of what makes Belle’s so much fun.”

For my husband and me, grilling lunch at Belle’s Camp was a fun change from the typical ski resort dining experience. It’s not every day you get to cook your own meal in the middle of one of the country’s most famous ski resorts.

If you love grilling your own lunch on the mountain, Vail isn’t your only option in Colorado.

Loveland Ski Area, near the Continental Divide, also lets skiers bring their own food and cook lunch without visiting a traditional restaurant.

The resort has four on-mountain cabins that the public can use for free, each equipped with propane grills. Visitors are welcome and encouraged to pack their own food and prepare a meal during their ski day.

It’s a particularly appealing option for families and groups who want a warm lunch without paying on-mountain restaurant prices. But beyond the savings, it’s also a fun way to slow down and enjoy a different side of skiing.

After all, some of the most memorable moments on the mountain don’t happen on the slopes. Sometimes, they’re as simple as grilling lunch with friends and family between runs.

#8235. Backyard Ultras Are Booming. Here’s Why.

In quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

It’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

Yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Big’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky new kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

For the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

We nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

It’s hard to take anything Nelson says seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

There is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Big’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

When Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Big, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

“The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell said. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now.  Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 New York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

Cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

He started Big’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he said. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

“I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he said. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”

The idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a big race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

“This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell said. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”

It’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell said this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Big’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell said, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Big’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”

Tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Big’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he said.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis said. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”

Lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

“Big’s is so great,” Lewis said. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”

Lewis races at Big’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Last year, he says his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis said.

This is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

“There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen said. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”

Katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”

Indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud said, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

“There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud said. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

But Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth said. “You get to see some amazing things.”

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

This year’s Big’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

Cantrell said there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

“I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell said. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”

But Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell said. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”

#8234. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.

#8233. Space Mirrors Promise Daylight in the Dark, But Rescue Teams Aren’t Convinced

A floodlight operated by Reflect Orbital illuminates the night sky. (Photo: Kern County Sheriff’s Office)

In the middle of a dark night on the foothills of Mt. Whitney, onlookers were suddenly flooded by a cone of light 3 miles wide by 10 miles long.

The source was a high-powered floodlight, placed nearby as part of a test exercise by a startup called Reflect Orbital. The Los Angeles-based company’s mission is to “launch the future of sunlight” by placing a swarm of mirrored satellites in low Earth orbit built to redirect sunlight anywhere on Earth on demand. The ground-based floodlight was designed to mimic that effect.

Among a wide range of use cases including agriculture, entertainment, and defense, the company claims rescue as one potential use of its tech in the coming years.

On a country road outside Lone Pine, California, a handful of seasoned rescue volunteers and public safety officials would find out how much — if any — a light field roughly the size of Manhattan and twice as bright as a full moon would improve their chances.

Phillip Cash, operations leader for China Lake Mountain Rescue Group, said his team arrived at the site with optimism.

“My team is largely scientists, engineers, technicians,” he told DarkSky International. “We live for this sort of stuff.”

Group leaders reported to the San Francisco Chronicle and DarkSky International that they envisioned very limited uses for the technology in rescue. They struggled with glare, saw little promise of benefit for helicopter crews, and realized the light could also shut off unexpectedly.

In the test, China Lake MRG and Inyo County SAR rehearsed standard search-and-rescue tasks twice — once in the dark, once under the big light. Crews ran grid searches, stretcher carries, and rope rigging.

Cash first noticed the light made it easier to move around on the ground. His peripheral vision was improved, he told DarkSky, and he didn’t have to worry about stepping in a hole.

But from there, the efficacy mostly faded.

Glare was an issue. While that may or may not be the case with a satellite as the source, Cash noted most rescuers already wear hats at night for this very reason. Limiting any light from the sky or ambient sources preserves night vision.

Another limiting factor of the test was that the organizers placed white pylons in the field as rescue targets, instead of the usual manikins. This created artificial reflectivity that helped Cash’s team find their marks more easily. But, he told DarkSky, his team realized the light could have a problematic effect on actual human subjects — especially anyone lost.

“They’re more likely to go, ‘Oh, look at all this light. Maybe I can find my way back now,’” he said.

Cash was also doubtful it would help SAR helicopter crews locate or navigate at night, noting they already use night vision as standard practice.

His takeaway: For the most part, it’s better to leave the daylight in the daytime.

“It’s not going to make a huge difference to wilderness search and rescue except in a few cases,” Cash told the Chronicle. “We’re pretty good at working at night already.”

Officials’ minds remain open to the technology. A spokesperson for the Kern County Sheriff’s Office told Backpacker that they intend to let SAR groups lead the way on any future implementation. That’s particularly the case with a team like China Lake MRG, a nonprofit that supports its equipment bills mainly through fundraising.

“Given the circumstances, if we needed it, it would definitely be something we would utilize,” said Lori Meza, Kern County Public Information Officer. “But we have no idea what it would cost.”

That price tag could be a real issue. While Reflect Orbital has not officially published any pricing information for its prospective services, Sky & Telescope reported that the company plans to charge around $5,000 per hour for its services, with constellations of multiple satellites — necessary to recreate the kind of bright conditions the team experienced — costing far more. (By comparison, an Airbus H125 helicopter, like the Kern County Sheriff’s Office operates, costs about $2,500 an hour to run, according to charter operator Craft.)

“Most search and rescue teams, at least in California, will not be able to afford it,” Cash told DarkSky. “They won’t even think about affording it. We cannot pay for that sort of thing.”

Emphasizing that any cost was still unknown, Meza said Kern County officials only buy equipment for SAR teams in limited cases. She gave the example of a purchase of vehicles several years ago.

“We do provide certain resources, and there might be an isolated case here or there,” she said. “But a purchase like a contracted service would be a new thing.”

She added that the Sheriff’s Office isn’t taking a position on the technology itself, and that they were grateful to be part of the test.

Other observers are less neutral. DarkSky International has functioned as a sort of public watchdog on Reflect Orbital, lobbying for what it sees as responsible development. Its five principles of outdoor lighting have been widely adopted, and published by the U.S. Department of Energy.

DarkSky sees the same gap in the technology for rescue as China Lake MRG — usefulness, which is also principle one of five.

“The first question is ‘is it needed?’” said Drew Reagan, DarkSky senior marketing and communications manager. “And in this case, the rescue groups found the need was pretty minimal.”

Many of the potential impacts of Reflect’s plan are unknown, because the government has allowed it to move forward with no environmental review.

If its plans become reality, the change in the night environment could be massive. The Federal Communications Commission has given the green light for Reflect to launch its first functional satellite. Its launch plan would place 50,000 in orbit by 2035. Even if they weren’t de facto floodlights, Reagan pointed out, the reflectivity of that many satellites alone would noticeably brighten the night sky everywhere on Earth.

“This represents a fundamentally new technology that will have a direct impact. Not only for the dark sky community or astrotourists, but for migratory birds, for insects,” Reagan said. “It’s not DarkSky’s goal to plunge the world into medieval darkness. We want to be part of these conversations. We just want to make sure we look before we launch.”

#8232. Lindsey Vonn Is Headed for Her 9th Surgery. She’s Still Thinking About Skiing.

Lndsey Vonn inspects the slope before the second official training for the women's downhill event at the Tofane Alpine Skiing Centre during Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games (Photo: Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images)

Lindsey Vonn is just days away from her ninth surgery in as many months, and the three-time Olympic medalist is still thinking about skiing.

On November 9, Vonn, 42, is heading into what’s slated to be the final surgery on her left leg following her severe crash during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in February. In an exclusive interview with Forbes, the alpine skier detailed her upcoming surgery.

“The plan is to remove all of the hardware, finally fix the ACL, and hopefully that’s my last surgery,” she told Forbes.

In February 2026, Vonn started the Olympic downhill race despite rupturing the ACL in her left knee just days earlier. After taking an aggressive line through the first few turns, Vonn clipped a gate just 13.4 seconds into her run, pushing her off course at the Tofane Alpine Skiing area.

The impact sent her spinning through the air before she crashed onto the icy surface, ending her race. Vonn was eventually airlifted to a hospital and diagnosed with complex fractures of the two bones in her lower left leg. Doctors put three plates and up to 20 screws in her leg, but couldn’t fix her ACL until her bones healed properly, she told Parade.

In the weeks following her initial surgery, Vonn shared that her injuries were so severe that she had to undergo an emergency fasciotomy, a procedure used to treat acute compartment syndrome. This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when pressure builds up around muscle groups, restricting blood flow or damaging muscles, tendons, and fascia. Colorado-based surgeon Dr. Tomas Hackett performed the complicated operation that saved her left leg from being amputated.

In a video shared to Instagram, the ski champion is sailing on a hydrofoil, writing that the event “was a big step in my recovery that made me incredibly happy. It may not have been snow but … it was one step closer to skiing.”

“I know I won’t be doing this, or much else, for quite some time after this next surgery, but I know I’ll get back to it,” she continued. “Eventually, I will.”

She said she expects to be on crutches for about four weeks and still has at least six months of rehabilitation in the works.

In 2010, Vonn became the first American woman to win Olympic gold in downhill skiing. Wherever she winds up, whether it’s slopeside or downhill, Vonn will always be our favorite comeback story.

#8231. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#8230. A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

#8227. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”
