#8210. 3 Expert-Approved Exercises to Build Power in Your Climbing

There’s a famous quote by Wolfgang Güllich, the German climber who invented the word “redpoint”: “There’s no such thing as too much power.” As a coach, I often see and hear this in the climbing community. I agree with the sentiment, but I think that by and large, power has been misused, misunderstood, and poorly trained by the vast majority of climbers.

Firstly, I think it’s misused and misunderstood because the general climbing population doesn’t grasp that strength and power are not the same thing. Secondly, as a result of this, the training methods climbers use when they’re trying to improve their power are often wrong.

So let’s start with a very simple explanation of strength and power. I’m also going to have to bring speed into the equation, as this gives context for how these all sit on a spectrum. Afterwards, we’ll look at some of the main things I think climbers are getting wrong when doing their own power training, how to solve these issues, and some examples of simple but effective ways to train power.

The reason that power matters so much in climbing is because not all moves are possible—or most efficient—when executed at a slower pace without speed and power. Trying to just use strength (slower movement) could mean that you’ll either fail on the move or you’ll climb inefficiently using excess energy, which ultimately means no send!

An easy example of this is completing a super long hard move. With just strength, we’re only able to lock to a certain depth of shoulder position and throw or deadpoint to a limited distance. Add in power and you’ll cover way more distance and end up latching that hold.

One additional note on the “power endurance” term: This one is a bit of a misnomer which caused us many issues over the years at Lattice, mainly because power endurance does not actually use power. It should have been named “strength endurance,” as that’s what it really is.

Strength is how much force you can produce. Think of a max hang on a small edge, or a heavy weighted pull-up. The movement is slow, but the force is high.

Speed is how fast you can move when there’s very little resistance. Think of how quickly you can move your hand from one hold to the next with only the weight of your own arm to overcome.

Power sits between the two. It’s force multiplied by speed, so you only have lots of it when you can produce a relatively high force quickly. Dynos, band-assisted pull-ups, and latching holds at the end of a deadpoint all fit into this category.

Think of it as a sliding scale. Heavy and slow climbing is at one end, light and fast climbing is at the other, and power is in the middle. You can’t produce your maximum force and your maximum speed at the same time, so where you train on that scale matters and I think climbers are continually getting this wrong.

None of this means strength doesn’t matter. Strength is the foundation of power. A stronger and bigger muscle can produce more force at every speed, so if you’re relatively weak, getting stronger will improve your power more than anything else. This is a really important point to grasp, for those of you who haven’t yet developed a foundation of high strength. Once you’re reasonably strong, though, specific power training starts to give you more benefits. As a rough guide, if you can’t do a pull-up with an extra 35-50% of your bodyweight, strength should be the main focus still (even though power training in addition is still useful). Once you’re above this threshold, power training should become increasingly important.

This is the big one. Power is extremely sensitive to fatigue and it drops well before you actually feel tired. Despite this, many climbers I see at the gym do their “power work” at the end of a session, after an hour of board climbing or a set of endurance drills. Unfortunately, if every rep is slower than your best, you’re practicing being slow. Power work goes at the start of the session, straight after a thorough warm-up, when you’re fresh. Prioritise this timing over everything.

Linked laps on the campus board, long sets of explosive pull-ups, and circuits of “powerful” moves can be useful, but they’re all mostly power endurance, not power. Power training means low numbers of high-quality reps. Stop the set as soon as a rep is noticeably slower, shorter, or messier than the first.

Ninety seconds between sets isn’t enough. You need at least three minutes, sometimes more, for the systems that drive maximal efforts to recover. If it feels like you’re resting way more than you should and you’re slightly bored, you’re probably resting the right amount.

The intention to move as fast as possible is a large part of what drives the adaptation, even when the movement itself ends up slow. So remember, if you’re doing a power pull-up, even if only the first 20% of the pull is fast, that’s ok. You should put in full intent, with complete focus on speed for each pull, and you’ll find that’s what really counts.

Some climbers only hang, push, squeeze, and lift heavy. Others love to campus, jump, spin, and dyno. The best results come from working across the scale. Heavy strength work (for the foundation of power and speed) and explosive power work should be included in the same training block, with the emphasis shifting depending on what you need for your goals.

Below are three power exercises that work well. Pick one or two for a session, do them first, and remember to stop as soon as speed or quality reduces.

If your 1RM pull-up is greater than 160%, you may be able to do this at bodyweight.

Pull as fast as possible, aiming to get your chest as high as possible, almost as if you’re trying to roll into a muscle up. Do four sets of three, resting three minutes between sets. The faster you can complete each rep, the better, so generally use more assistance than you might think.

Always learn how to do this session on a comfortable hold and using your preferred grip type.

Using a hangboard edge (or a load cell, if you have one), pull as hard and as fast as you can for two to three seconds. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between. This trains your ability to generate high force quickly, which is exactly what deadpoints need.

These can be done on holds, a hangboard, or a pull-up bar. The critical part is getting the height of the starting position right.

Using your chosen hold, you want to jump from the ground into the middle range of the pull-up motion, using the momentum from your lower body to assist in generating speed and power in the upper part of the pull. You’re jumping into the pull-up with your legs, and your arms and back are finishing off the pull at high speed as you’re already carrying momentum. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between.

Train power like this two to three times a week when it’s your focus, and once or twice a week to maintain it the rest of the time. Don’t forget that power fades faster than strength when you stop training it, so it’s worth keeping a small amount in your plan all year round.

So back to Güllich: Is there such a thing as too much power? Probably not. But there’s definitely such a thing as too much fatigue, too much volume, and too little speed and intention when you’re trying to train it. Get strong first, train power fresh in mind and body, keep the quality high, and stop before it drops. I think you’ll be pretty happy with how you feel on the wall after just a couple of months of this.

#8209. You Don’t Need ‘Pervert Glasses’ to Remember Your Hike

A woman is holding a pair of smart glasses from Ray-Ban Meta in her hand at an eyewear store. Because these glasses allow users to take photos and videos, some outdoor and indoor swimming pools are considering banning them. (Photo: Christoph Schmidt/picture alliance via Getty Images)

In the annals of uncool accessories—the pocket protector, the cell phone holster, cargo shorts—smart glasses have already earned a place of special scorn. Unlike those utilitarian pieces, the backlash against the high-tech glasses isn’t about what they look like, though their oversized temples and chunky frames do give them a distinct Spirit Halloween look. It’s what they do: Their ability to record anyone the user looks at has led governments from Norway to New York to consider restrictions and businesses like theaters and bars to ban them. After several well-publicized incidents of users deploying smart glasses to covertly film women on the street, some detractors have labeled the wearables “pervert glasses.”

Despite that stigma, Meta, the company behind both Facebook and the most popular models of smart glasses, reportedly sold 7 million pairs of them in 2025 alone, and the eyewear has become a regular sight everywhere from bike paths to restaurants. Now, Meta wants you to take them on your next hike.

In a patent application published on October 15, Meta outlined a software update for its product that would use contextual clues like audio, speech, and data from wearables to automatically edit video captured by the glasses. The first use case the company offered: Creating a highlight reel from a recording of a hike. For example, if the glasses record the sound of a waterfall or the user saying “Look at that bird,” they could tag the footage from that moment as significant; likewise if, for example, a connected smartwatch registers your heart rate spiking. While those automatic features are still pending, hiking footage shot on the Meta glasses abounds on YouTube.

Exactly how much of the internet that search would have scoured is an open question: The company reportedly contemplated both limiting it to a user’s friends and allowing it to search everyone with a profile on Meta platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and Threads. While Meta quietly removed the software after Wired’s report, it’s been mum on its future plans for the technology, and third-party researchers have demonstrated how easy it is to livestream footage from the glasses into existing facial recognition engines. It’s easy to imagine a worst-case scenario where a stranger passing by could learn an uncomfortable amount about your life without ever saying a word. (While a built-in LED signals when the glasses are recording, some regulators have noted that it is not easily visible in bright sunlight, and models from many lesser-known manufacturers don’t have any kind of indicator.)

One might ask: Is any of this worth it? Meta has spent tens of millions of dollars lobbying the government not to regulate it. Is letting it ride shotgun on your hike like some real-life episode of Black Mirror a good idea? Will anyone actually look at the hundreds of thousands of hours of video these glasses capture, or will it just gather dust in a data center somewhere like most of the footage people shoot on their phones? (To be fair, I’ll also note here that smart glasses have been a game-changing tool for their small population of blind and low-vision users—about 8 percent of buyers cite accessibility as their main reason, according to a report by Security.org—though they don’t seem to be the demographic Meta is serving with these proposed software updates.) But I’m not here to judge how other hikers use tech. I’m more concerned with how it affects everyone else.

The backcountry means something different to every hiker, but to a lot of us, it’s an escape—from responsibilities, from city noise, and, increasingly, from being watched. We live today in a world that’s more monitored and recorded than ever before: Between automatic license plate readers, Ring doorbells, dash cams, and commercial security systems, an average urban dweller might feasibly spend their entire day hopping from one camera’s field of view to another. The backcountry is one of the last unsurveilled environments in North America; with the glasses’ new capabilities, Meta proposes to introduce what’s rapidly becoming a face-mounted Flock camera into it.

Whether we’re talking about smart glasses, stealth camping, or hiking with off-leash dogs, discussions about how we behave in the backcountry often devolve into arguments about individual freedom and responsibility. That misses the point: There are some behaviors that affect the experience of everyone around us. The person who decides to film their hike with a wearable that monitors everything they see and hear reaps all the benefits of that decision; it’s other backpackers that I foresee bearing the cost. Nor are those costs evenly distributed: A YouGov poll found that roughly two-thirds of people interested in buying smart glasses are men, while the Security study found that women are consistently more likely to report concern about the glasses’ cameras and potential facial recognition tech.

Someone will likely read this and ask what the big deal is; anyone with a phone, after all, can already record anyone they please. But there’s a big difference between pointing a camera at another person and being able to record anyone you look at, let alone run them through face ID. The trail is where backpackers feel the most unburdened—the least obligated to perform the roles we inhabit in our everyday lives. When anyone with a pair of shades could be recording you, living freely may start to feel a lot less sustainable.

#8208. The Warmest Gloves and Mittens for People Who Get Cold Easily

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

(Photo: Courtesy of Columbia, Gordini, and Swany)

If you’re anything like me, winter is a catch-22. On the one hand, it’s the season for skiing, so I love it dearly. On the other hand, I live in a perpetual state of cold hands.

I have pretty poor circulation, and as a result, my fingers and toes turn icy rather quickly. That’s why the gloves and mittens I wear need to be extra warm. I’ve found that while gloves are easier to grip ski poles with, I’ll trade a bit of dexterity for the extra warmth that mittens provide.

If you also suffer from cold hands, then look no further. We partnered with SKI testers and editors to round up seven of the gloves and mittens they have found to be warmest. From heated options to gloves under $100, this is the ultimate list for keeping your fingers toasty even on the coldest of days.

Outdoor Research Sureshot Heated Soft-Shell Gloves

Sizes: XS–XL (unisex) Shell: Leather and nylon Insulation: Recycled featherless 3M Thinsulate, Polartec Power Grid fleece

Pros and Cons + Handy cuff pull loop + Durable goat leather and nylon shell + Fleecy lining – Some break-in required

Testers found Mainers Mitts to be some of the warmest non-heated mittens. The waterproof Gore-Tex liner keeps hands dry and wicks away moisture, while the recycled “featherless” 3M Thinsulate insulation adds plenty of warmth—without the bulk.

While the mittens did require several wears to break in, SKI testers noted that the lack of bulk helped the mittens’ dexterity. Even testers who prefer gloves were impressed by the mitt’s flexibility.

The parent company of Mainers, Tempshield, makes PPE for laboratories involved with cryogenics and has scientists working in temperatures below −200°F, so you can rest assured knowing Mainers knows how to keep your hands warm.

Sizes: 7–11 (unisex) Shell: Leather Insulation: PrimaLoft Gold

Pros and Cons + Soft and durable full leather shell + Padded fingers and back of hand + Velcro cuff easily tucks under jacket – Water-resistant, not waterproof

This LEKI glove is crafted with one of the warmest synthetic materials, PrimaLoft Gold (100 percent polyester). Testers loved how grippy the glove is and gave high marks for nimbleness. Testers also noted the gloves work with smartphone screens.

A neoprene backing and leather shell will protect hands from high wind chill, but it’s important to note the gloves are not 100 percent waterproof. Instead, they’re water resistant, so it’s best to leave them at home on wet spring days.

Sizes: S–XL (men’s); S–L (women’s) Shell: Waxed leather Insulation: Aquablock Down, high-pile fleece

Pros and Cons + Breathable, not clammy + Supple leather + Neoprene undercuff with hook-and-loop closure – Leather is hard to wash

What sets Gordini’s Alp Pro Mitt apart from the competition is its waxed leather, which keeps heat in and moisture out.

SKI testers loved the mitten’s breathability and found that even when temperatures started to rise, hands didn’t go clammy. The waxed leather exterior keeps the elements out and also preserves the mitten’s lifespan so you can use it year after year. The interior is a mixture of down and fleece, so hands remain warm without overheating.

One tester even went so far as to call the mittens one of the nicest they’ve ever worn.

The mitten’s strongest asset is also a weakness: the waxed leather makes them harder to clean, so perhaps use a tissue instead of a mitten for wiping up messes.

Sizes: S–XL (men’s); XS–XL (women’s) Shell: Polyester with goatskin leather palm Insulation: 200g recycled and virgin polyester

Pros and Cons + Great value + Men’s and women’s sizes + Articulated fit – Run small

The PowBound gloves may lack some of the bells and whistles of the more expensive options on our list, but they do have two of the most important factors: weather protection and polyester insulation.

Testers noted that the gloves are likely not going to last as long as some of the others on this list, but they’ll be sturdy for at least a few seasons. Other pros are the wrist straps, so you can guarantee no gloves will be dropped from the chairlift, and a handy clip to keep them from running off solo.

Testers also noted the gloves run a little snug, so when in doubt, size up.

Sizes: 6–11 (unisex) Shell: Cowhide, neoprene cuff Insulation: Foam

Pros and Cons + Removable liners + Ultra burly + Comes with leashes and wrist grommets with carabiner for easy clipping – Requires break-in period

If you look closely, you’ll find Hestra gloves being sported at almost any resort—they’re the popular kid for a reason.

SKI testers voted the Fall Line glove from Hestra “most rugged” because of the materials that go into keeping hands warm and dry all day long. The exterior is composed of cowhide and treated with leather balm to create a barrier against the elements. Hestra gloves also come with a mini tube of said leather balm so you can treat your gloves as needed.

The interior of the glove is composed of brushed polyester and foam, which helps insulate chilly fingers without overheating. Small details, like a seam over the fingertips, help to reduce pressure points, and when you’re holding a pole tightly, that’s a noticeable difference.

The one downfall SKI testers noted was that the glove can feel a bit stiff when fresh out of the packaging, and the Fall Line requires some love before it comes nice and soft.

Sizes: XS–XL (unisex) Battery Life: 8 hours on low, 4 hours on normal, 3 hours on high, 2 hours on boost; dual battery capacity

Pros and Cons + Also available in a mitt + High-quality leather + No battery removal for charging – Charger can get disconnected easily – Not touchscreen compatible

As one of two heated options on this list, we figured we had to mention SKI testers’ best heated glove overall. The Swany Nexus Heated Glove isn’t cheap, but for those who suffer from cold hands, it’s well worth the hefty price tag.

Testers raved about the glove’s ewool, a new technology that delivers heat to each finger, all the way to the fingertips. The PrimaLoft insulation and the leather shell don’t add much bulk. The glove’s lightweight density and soft feel had testers noting that the glove was both the warmest and most comfortable of the bunch.

Best of all, you don’t need to remove the batteries to charge the gloves; there’s a built-in port on the cuff of the glove. Plus, they’re TSA-compliant, so you can keep them in your carry-on bag.

Sizes: S–XL (men’s); S–L (women’s) Battery Life: 8 hours on low, 5 hours on medium, 2.25 hours on high

Pros and Cons + Zippered gauntlet cuff + Very low profile + Exceptionally breathable – Not for the coldest temperatures

While most of the gloves and mittens on this list are made for cold outdoor pursuits, the Sureshot from Outdoor Research is for everyday use. Frigid dog walks, games in outdoor stadiums, and nights by the campfire are all perfect occasions for a heated glove that isn’t meant for extreme temperatures or hardcore activities. Unlike many other heated gloves on the market, these are even touchscreen compatible.

The two-layer woven stretch exterior means the gloves are water- and wind-resistant. And even though the gloves aren’t 100 percent waterproof, the synthetic insulation kept hands warm even when the gloves were wet.

Testers noted that the smaller wrist batteries were barely noticeable, and on the lowest setting, the gloves will produce heat for eight full hours.

#8205. A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey)

In 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing soaring rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

“To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there isn’t a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Outside.

That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) launched a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

“People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett said.

As part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

“You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett said. “Just take pictures.”

Nearly one in ten Americans have mobility issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett says enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

“For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett said.

Kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people plan their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

“We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”

The map includes 50 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that shows the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

The tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as New Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

BLM’s new map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

Gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

“Trails are kind of living things,” Ray said. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”

Move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray said.

“If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she said. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”

For trail users like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she says, it never will.

“I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett says. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”

She added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

“Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett said. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”

#8204. The Best Ice Climbing Gear of 2027: Boots, Tools, Crampons, and More

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The author, Anthony Walsh, heads up 'Nightmare on Wolfstreet' (WI6 M7+) on B.C.'s famed Stanley Headwall. (Photo: Sebastian Pelletti)

Overview: The best ice climbing gear of 2027 includes Petzl Dart crampons, La Sportiva Olympus Mons Pro boots, Black Diamond Viper ice tool, the Blue Ice Choucas Pro harness, and the Mountain Equipment Xenith jacket, plus proven picks like the La Sportiva G-Summit boots. Our testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 from the Canadian Rockies to the Patagonian Andes, in temperatures down to -30°F.

Ice climbing is a high-stakes sport. Do it right, and you’re in for a meditative cruise with just the right level of spice. Do it wrong, and you’ll be left spooked, shivering—or worse. The difference often boils down to your experience level. But right after that comes your ice climbing gear. When you’re 100 feet off the ground, pinned to a silvery ribbon of ice by nothing but four blades of steel, you need absolute trust in your equipment. But how can you tell which products to rely on? That’s our job.

This season, our team of testers tried out 15 pieces of ice climbing gear that are either new for 2026-’27 or came out partway through last winter. Some turned out to be overengineered, overpriced, or poorly built. Others proved thoughtfully designed and dependable in a range of winter conditions. Over thousands of vertical feet of testing everywhere from the Patagonian Andes to the Canadian Rockies, we sorted out the bad from the good. Below: nothing but the best ice climbing gear available this season.

Weight: 11.3 oz (men’s medium) / 9.9 oz (women’s medium)

Pros and Cons + Novel and effective baffle design + Two-way zipper with bottom hem snap + Low-profile, elasticated cuffs + Impressive warmth-to-weight ratio – No way to tighten hood – Gimmicky and impractical hexagonal stuff sack

Mountain Equipment’s all-new Xenith is the big experiment in winter insulation this year. After a research paper suggested hexagons might be the most thermally efficient shape, the brand built the jacket with hexagonal baffles. (These weirdly shaped baffles also seem to limit down migration.)

Our testers found it extremely warm for 11.3 ounces (with 4.3 ounces of 800-fill hydrophobic goose down)—making it the ideal midlayer on -30°F days and nearly unnoticeable clipped to a harness on warmer ones. The Xenith’s low weight comes from its spare design. It has two hand-warming pockets, elasticated cuffs, a two-way zipper, internal drop pockets, a hem-cinch cord, and a hood. Downside: The hood can’t be cinched at all. Without a helmet to fill it, you’ll feel like a kid wearing your parent’s oversized clothes.

Weight: 8.5 oz Sizes: men’s XXS-XXL (the women’s counterpart is the M10 Storm Bib)

Pros and Cons + Surprising stretch and durability + Superior range of motion – No women’s-specific version

The M10 Storm Hardshell offers hands-down the best range of motion we’ve ever experienced in an alpine climbing pant. Thanks to a roomy fit, gusseted crotch, and slightly stretchy fabric—a mix of ripstop nylon, proprietary waterproof laminate, and a slick jersey backer—we were able to step high and wide without feeling constricted—a refreshing departure from the Euro-style, slim-fit trousers that have taken over the market in recent years.

“While transitioning from a panel of limestone to a hanging ice dagger, I stemmed my legs as far as I could between the two mediums and felt zero resistance,” reported Climbing senior editor Anthony Walsh. Some testers reported doing a full split just to test out the mobility. No torn crotches yet.

The rest of the layout is smart but simple. The thigh pocket, big enough to fit a smartphone, and fly are both positioned to remain accessible even with a harness on. “The zipper is on a diagonal rather than vertically-oriented like most other pants, so you can relieve yourself without a harness’s tie-in points or belay loop getting in the way,” Walsh reports. Elasticized cuffs keep moisture out—something we appreciated when spring conditions left our ice pitches streaming with water.

We loved how waterproof the M10s were, too. “I tested the M10s on some of the wettest pitches of my entire season,” said Walsh. “My ‘waterproof’ gloves soon wetted out, and my face had a steady drip of water coming off my nose, but under the M10 pants, I stayed 100 percent dry.” Credit goes to a lightweight, breathable, proprietary membrane and a PFCs-free DWR (durable water repellent) that boasted best-in-test longevity. After eight straight days of fighting up scrappy mixed lines in the Canadian Rockies, both the waterproofing and the fabric remained intact.

Pros and Cons + Legitimately waterproof + Decently breathable + Cuff closure keeps out loose snow – Not very warm

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

The Temres is not exceedingly warm, but for temps hovering around freezing (or those with excellent circulation) these are a fantastic, cheap option. Otherwise, buy a larger size and add a thin liner glove for deep-winter leads. A note on sizing: Showa gloves run small, so size one up from your typical ice glove.

Pros and Cons + Warmest technical mountaineering boot made + Easy adjustment with BOA system + Surprisingly nimble and lightweight – Expensive – Unnecessarily tall gaiter

Knee-height mountain boots are no longer just for guided Himalayan climbers. La Sportiva’s new Olympus Mons Pro—a 4-pound-4-ounce pair of “8,000-meter boots”—is a game changer for ice and mixed climbers who need serious warmth without sacrificing performance.

Our tester wore them on Field of Dreams (WI5; 250ft), Mixed Master (WI4 M5; 1,000ft), and M7 cragging. “I have generally cold feet yet I was sweating standing around in -5°F in these boots,” he said. “Despite all the insulation, these are plenty nimble for WI5 and M5.” The Olympus Mons Pro might be a couple ounces heavier than La Sportiva’s G-Summit boot, but it is drastically warmer and just as comfortable. Unbelievably, it’s also 7 ounces lighter per pair than the brand’s flagship leather single boot, the Nepal EVO, thanks to Primaloft Gold Aerogel insulation.

The one gripe: an unnecessarily tall gaiter. “With such a long zipper to get in and out of the boot, I’m less likely to adjust the Velcro power strap when I need to,” said one tester. Thankfully the external BOA allows a climber to adjust some of the fit on the fly.

Weight: 1 lb 13 oz (per boot) Sizes: 37-48 (half sizes)

Pros and Cons + Easy to adjust with gloves on + Highly versatile + Ideal fit for small and low-volume feet – Not as durable as they should be for the price

The G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

“I loved the BOA system for quick tightening mid-pitch and for equally quick loosening when I arrived at the next belay and needed blood to rush into my feet,” said Climbing Senior Editor Anthony Walsh, who was able to operate the dial easily with gloves on. The system eliminated heel-lift, both on-route and off. “I’ve front-pointed 10,000 feet in these boots and walked many horizontal miles. I haven’t received one blister, and yet I can still climb WI6 and M7 in them,” Walsh said.

Our female testers raved about the fit, calling it a serious game-changer in a world dominated by men’s boots. “Not only does this accommodate lower-volume feet, but the BOA ratchets tight enough to keep my heel down,” said one woman. “That allows me to climb a lot harder, for a lot longer.”

The boot isn’t totally waterproof, but its TPU coating, weather-resistant zipper, and water-repellant finishes kept our feet dry after dozens of days on ice and snow. “Lots of approaches in the Rockies have semi-frozen rivers at the base,” said one tester. “I punched through multiple, and never felt humidity or wetness.”

But while the weather resistance easily survives hard use, some of the plastic parts may not. One tester noted a sticky zipper and a peeling toe cap. Another reported that the toe welt quickly shows signs of wear and had to order a replacement after just a few weeks of testing. The toe welts on her second pair have held up fine. Still, if you’re hoping for a boot that will last you for years, you might want to get some reassurances from La Sportiva’s warranty department first.

Pros and Cons + Top-tier durability + Technical aptitude + Out-of-the-box comfort – Not quite warm enough for extreme-altitude objectives

Scarpa’s fan-favorite Phantom Tech HD offers the same climbing precision as the old Phantom Tech, with more warmth, durability, and comfort at just a 2.5-ounce penalty. Body-mapped insulation—micropile, aerogel, and PrimaLoft Gold Eco—kept our feet frostbite-free at -22°F (with vapor barrier socks) near Field, British Columbia, but we wouldn’t quite trust it on Denali. “The rockered outsole has a trail-runner-like feel,” said one tester. “I’ve hiked and skied many miles in ice climbing boots over the years, and the Phantom Tech HD is without a doubt the most comfortable I’ve used.” After a full season, our pair shows no wear or delamination.

Pros and Cons + Packable + Superlight + Five gear loops – Uncomfortable to hang in – Ice clipper locations reduce usability of gear loops

For multi-pitch ice, where hanging belays are rare, our testers gravitate to a minimalist harness like the updated Blue Ice Choucas Pro. Its UHMWPE construction is surprisingly durable for 5.1 ounces, and it’s fully featured: gear loops, a haul loop, four ice clipper slots, and leg loops that open for skis or crampons.

Unfortunately, Blue Ice sewed the clipper slots over the gear loops, so loop real estate feels a bit scarce. Nevertheless, it easily held a full rack of screws on Murchison Falls (WI4+; 600ft), but our tester noticed the unpadded leg loops on the free-hanging 100-foot rappel.

Skip it for cragging or steep terrain; it thrives on big days in the alpine—where a harness’s weight and packability make a real difference.

Pros and Cons + IP56 water resistance + Low operating limit (-20°F) + Invaluable for anchors and belay-station communication – Expensive

An IP56 water-resistance rating and a -20°F lower operating limit make the Rocky Talkies as well suited to ice as to the mountains they’re named for. We found them invaluable for setting up anchors in Ouray Ice Park and for communicating between multi-pitch belay stations. The only knock is the price, though most testers found the durability worth it.

Pros and Cons + Long-lasting dry treatment + Easy handling – No middle mark

If you’re the kind of person who prefers the safety and flexibility of a half/twin rope setup, you’d be hard-pressed to do better than the DYAD 7.7. Our testers used these ropes on everything from Bridal Veil Falls to ice park laps over a full season in Ouray, Colorado, and not even the wettest pitches iced them up or wetted them out. Cons: There’s no middle mark, and the ropes are pricey.

Pros and Cons + Many accessories for specific customization + High-performance ice pick – Shaft shape and handle is not suited for sustained vertical or overhanging pitches

Gently curved ice tools have fallen out of favor for the flashier, radically shaped Black Diamond Hydra, but the updated Viper still has a home in our quiver. Its 2.5-millimeter pick is incredible in ice, but the tool’s standout feature is its customization: it comes with modular headweights, a long alpine spike for snow plunging, a micro spike, a full-size alpine hammer, a micro hammer, and an adze. One tester, an ACMG apprentice alpine guide, found the mellow shape natural for sniffing out thin hooks on slabby, traddy mixed up to M7, versus an aggressive tool like the C.A.M.P. X-Dream. The knuckle-bashing shape isn’t ideal for overhanging mixed or WI5, but it’s a great option for moderate and big-mountain routes.

Weight: 1 lb 9 oz (per pair, with monopoint setup) Sizes: 34-44; 38-49 with extension bar (sold separately)

+ Extremely light + Solid climbing performance + Surprisingly durable + Wide range of adjustability – Aluminum heel doesn’t penetrate dense ice well

With razor-sharp points and a modular design, the Petzl Dart has been our favorite technical crampon for years. Its new aluminum rear section and linking bar save 4 ounces per pair and eliminate the need to jerry-rig fit with Petzl’s Cord-Tec Kit.

Testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 with zero flex or shifting. Like the all-steel Dart, it’s simple to switch between mono- and dual-point layouts, and interchangeable toe bails customize the Dart for any boot, welts or not. Testers used these ‘pons on everything from Bridalveil Falls (WI5+) in Telluride and hard mixed cragging to big Canadian Rockies north faces, including Mount Robson and Mount Temple.

The geometry of the front point is just downturned enough to hook securely into ice, but not so aggressive that you have to adjust your technique to get a solid stick. In fact, most testers found they hardly had to double-kick at all to get a quick, reliable bite.

“The secondary points are far enough back that they don’t get in your way when you just want to use your front point, but forward enough to engage when you want them to,” said one tester, who wore them on more than 100 pitches this winter. He also found them blessedly intuitive to walk in: “Even when hiking up and down the Ouray Ice Park trails or navigating a mixture of rocks and ice between backcountry pitches, the Darts kept me secure and balanced.”

Cons: Honestly, not many. One climber found the newly slimmed-down heel lever tough to operate with thick gloves on. Another found the metal buckle fussy—though Petzl’s sold-separately Elastic Strap ($26) fixes that issue with a surprisingly durable plastic buckle.

Pros and Cons + Triple-grip handle + Flexibility and reach in steep terrain – Too aggressive for pure ice – Handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as other triple-grip models

One climbing coach and U.S. Ice Climbing Team member used the X-Dream Total Dry on hard mixed routes in Ouray and D14 king lines in the Italian Dolomites. The first widely available commercial tool with a triple-grip handle, it gives you tons of flexibility and reach in steep terrain. But it’s too aggressive for pure ice, and the handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as on other triple-grip models. Thankfully, the X-Dream’s all-around handle is available separately.

Pros and Cons + Modular head weights + Ultra-sharp picks + Adjustable handle size – Geometry isn’t aggressive enough for seriously overhung terrain

An impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. “I certainly appreciated being able to adjust the handle size to accommodate the difference,” said one tester, who swapped between thin dry-tooling gloves and thick, three-finger mitts. The geometry isn’t aggressive enough for overhung mixed, though, like the crux ice-dagger transfer on Dark Nature (WI5+ M5/6).

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Durable steel + Seamless rotation + Easy to place – Spring-loaded crank knobs are sometimes overeager

We occasionally steer clear of aluminum screws because we find they bind up in plasticky ice. But the featherweight, all-steel Blue Ice Aeros are easily the next best thing. The lightest steel screw on the market, the Aeros are easy to start, easy to clean, and rack neatly on a harness. The three-tooth design seems to bite more reliably than four-toothed models, and we found the Aeros never bound up, even in warm, snowy conditions in Colorado’s Ouray Ice Park.

Ease of racking was another fan-favorite perk. You can fit six screws on a single clipper as opposed to Black Diamond or Petzl’s four to five. Credit goes to the low-profile aluminum hangers, which Blue Ice managed to trim down without sacrificing the size of the crank knob or the length of the hanger.

“The hangers are long enough to provide plenty of torque to easily turn the screw, and they’re simple to manipulate with gloves,” said one Colorado-based tester after a season of backcountry ascents in the San Juans.

The Aeros also offer a larger barrel diameter than any other screw we’ve tried, which means you can thread them into old screw holes in a pinch and still get a tight, reliable placement. The larger diameter also came in handy while setting up rappels.

“V-threading was a breeze with the Aero, providing a wide window of ice to thread the rope and get it back out with my V-thread tool,” reported one tester.

The only thing we didn’t like was the spring-loaded crank knobs. While some testers loved that they snap back into the screw automatically, others found that the snapping sometimes occurred prematurely, pinching their fingers or gloves in the process.

Buy in this order: boots, layers, gloves, then a big belay parka. Crampons, ice tools, and screws are easy to rent or borrow while you’re learning. Boots and apparel aren’t, and they matter most to your comfort on the ice.

Start with boots, because fit is everything.

You can find used boots for $200 to $300, but buy new if that’s what it takes to get a perfect fit. Visit a local climbing shop, tell the sales associate about your objectives and experience level, and let them guide you.

Layer for the conditions, and keep your insulation adjustable.

Carry two to three pairs. Wet hands are cold hands, so the number-one tip for staying comfortable is keeping your mitts dry. You’ll need:

As with boots, buy your gloves new if that’s what it takes to get the fit right.

Yes, eventually. Make it the last piece of your kit. A two-way zipper and interior drop pockets are nice, but warmth matters most. Standing around belaying in the snow can be downright frigid, and the bigger and warmer your belay puffy, the happier you’ll be.

Rent or borrow these until you know what you like:

Yes, but upgrade as you get more into the sport.

Buy safety essentials new. That means ropes, harnesses, and helmets. It’s hard to tell if used gear has been compromised, and trustworthy safety gear is the cheapest insurance policy you’ll ever buy.

For most other items, shopping secondhand can help you figure out what you like before you shell out for a spendy new kit. Try MountainProject.com, GearTrade.com, and eBay, or Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace if you live in an outdoorsy town.

Gear reviews are highly subjective, but we do our best to combat that by taking a slightly more scientific approach to testing ice climbing gear. At the beginning of each season, we wade through sheaves of PR requests, consider the specs and promise of each one, and then carefully select the gear we deem fit to test. Then, we do our utmost to get each piece in the hands of as many testers as we can—and in as varied conditions as the team can manage.

This year, testers picked and kicked their way up everything from steep ice in Colorado’s San Juans to long mixed lines on Mount Robson. Samples traveled from Denali to the Italian Dolomites to the Patagonian Andes and back again. We belayed through blizzards, swung into bullet-hard ice, whooped over perfect sticks, and cursed through some of the wettest pitches of our lives. At the end of the year, we compared notes and selected only the best ice climbing gear to review. Those are the products you’ll see here.

Anthony Walsh is a senior editor at Climbing. Based in the Canadian Rockies, he does it all—from steep ice to long alpine routes to rowdy mixed climbs. All those pitches have helped him hone two unmatched talents: suffering honorably in Arctic conditions, and complaining about poorly constructed gear in the most eloquent way possible.

Corey Buhay is a freelance writer and editor based in Boulder, Colorado. She is a current member of the U.S. Ice Climbing Team and has redpointed up to WI5, M12-, and D14 around the Colorado Rockies and beyond. She is a coach and board member at The Ice Coop, Colorado’s only dedicated ice-climbing gym.

Emilie Grenier is a regular contributor to Climbing who actually prefers climbing ice to rock. As a result, Emilie is hunting for frozen smears come September each year, and you can’t drag her out of crampons until at least May.

#8203. Think Your Pack Is Heavy? This Hiker Carries 220 Pounds For Fun

On a Saturday in Slovakia’s Tatra Mountains, Regan Bridge stood in a line of tourists at the foot of a cliff studded with ladders and chains. Strapped to his back was his own 120-liter army pack, stuffed with 132 pounds of supplies. A carry strap ran across his forehead. “It was ugly,” he says.

He couldn’t get the pack up the ladder, so Bridge did what nobody was supposed to do and climbed the chains on the path designated for the descent, in full view of the local porters, who are famous for hauling extraordinary weights.

When he hikes back home in New Zealand, 54-year-old Bridge’s setup looks like a stunt. Toolboxes stacked high, a ladder, and up to 220 pounds adorn the back of the log truck driver. Up close, he is the opposite of a stuntman: He has no social media and makes no money from his hobby.

I write about ultralight gear, so on paper Bridge and I don’t have much in common. I carry light, while he hauls as much as he can. He gets jokes from passersby about bringing the whole house, and I get asked whether my boyfriend is carrying my sleeping bag. But we’ve both learned how easily others can misconstrue the way we pack, and how little that has to do with why we do it.

Having previously been involved in stone lifting, Bridge was no stranger to unusual tests of strength. His interest in carrying heavy loads in the backcountry began when he volunteered to transport 15 predator traps for a New Zealand conservation project. Typically, workers were only allowed to haul two at a time. Bridge asked for the rule to change; the organization waived its weight limit for him, and he cleared them all in two trips. The experience expanded his sense of what the human body could manage. “It grew my mindset,” he says, and he began looking for new ways to test it.

Since then, Bridge has slowly piled on more weight. His setup includes duplicate hiking gear, even multiple pairs of footwear, to maximize the load. The toolboxes hold water bottles, which he empties at the summit, roughly halving his load for the descent. He uses the ladder to get the pack on and off and to rest along the way; once it exceeds 110 pounds (50 kilograms), he can no longer lift it off the ground himself. Bridge admits he now favors steep, demanding dayhikes for the adrenaline rush; longer, multiday trips have lost their appeal.

After watching a documentary about Slovakia’s nosiči, the mountain porters who carry supplies to remote huts, Bridge traveled there hoping to experience it for himself. His wife of 25 years found a place that offered tourists the chance to carry supplies between huts in exchange for a free coffee. The suggested load was 44 pounds, or 20 kilos. “I looked at that and went, I ain’t carrying no 20 kilos.”

Instead, Bridge carried double the suggested weight up to the top hut on the first day, and was rewarded with coffee and rum, which, he says, “made that trip down really fun.” The following day his climb up the chains caught the porters’ attention. They offered him a turn carrying their traditional frame, laden with 110 pounds.

“They’re probably stepping out on a limb to give me a go,” he reflects. When he told them he did this for fun back home, they thought he was “a little bit crazy.” But among the porters, he was no oddity. He was “a dime a dozen.”

People can be quick to judge. Other hikers tell him it’s a waste of time; others warn his knees won’t last. “And I’m looking at them going, well, you’re tramping [hiking]. That’s a waste of time too.”

“I want to live. I want to do stuff,” he says. “If I have to get a knee done when I’m 60, I’ll get a knee done.”

He likes the history behind the porters’ work, but says, “I also like the space it puts me in while I’m doing it.” Climbing is his favorite part. “The climb just clears my brain a bit more, but I still have the chance to think about where I am, have a look at the view.” Descents are different; he’s too focused on not getting hurt. I’d pictured a stoic, silent grind; instead, he hauls to a soundtrack ranging from AC/DC to ’90s dance music. Asked what keeps him coming back, Bridge describes it as “just feeding the soul.”

Next, he wants to take 220 pounds (100 kilograms) up the 2,200 steps of the Sealy Tarns Track in Aoraki National Park. But his carefully balanced setup makes exposed climbs tricky.:“You put wind in there, it’s diabolical.”

Before we hung up, Regan pulled out the questions I’d sent ahead of our interview, which he’d printed, and went through them to ensure we’d covered everything. He wanted the facts right, because through translation, things can change.

“All of a sudden, I’m carrying 120 kilos (264 pounds),” he says. “I don’t want people to think that I’ve done something that I haven’t.”

He has no sponsors and no followers, yet he still wanted every number right—no flattering angle, no bigger feat, just a man who didn’t want credit for a kilo he hadn’t carried.

When the call ended, Bridge was off to spend an hour training, as he does six days a week. I’d asked him earlier whether there would ever be a peak, a weight where he’d say, “that’s enough”.

“One day I’m going to wake up and go, yep, I’m there. I’m happy,” he says. “And until then, it’s still going to continue to be fun.”

#8199. Here Is What an After-Dinner Walk Actually Does to Your Sleep, According to a Board-Certified Doctor

Here’s a scenario many of us know too well: we eat a plate the size of a hubcap, then lose a fight with the couch by halftime. That slump has a name: postprandial somnolence, or what some people call a “food coma,” and it has a real biological basis.

As Outside previously reported, the smart move after a big dinner is a short, easy walk or “fart walk,” which helps food move through the digestive system—and may also help you get a good night’s rest.

I’m a board-certified internal medicine doctor; here’s how a walk, whether you decide to take a walk on your favorite trail or hit the treadmill, after a good meal may induce sleep.

Growing up, I was told that a big meal makes you sleepy because your stomach steals blood from your brain to digest the food. While digestion does pull extra blood to the gut, the brain guards its own supply closely, so blood flow isn’t the main reason you’re getting tired. Scientists now think a food coma results from several things piling up at once.

In lab studies, people got drowsier in the hours after eating, even when researchers accounted for the time of day and whatever was on the plate. Your internal clock dips in the early afternoon whether you eat or not, reducing performance. Sleep loss at night adds to the drowsiness, and so does a glass or two of wine. In experiments in mice, signals from a full stomach travel up the vagus nerve, a long nerve running from the brain to the gut, and switch on calming brain cells. Whether the same thing happens in people is still unknown.

What we do know is that some of the slump is out of your hands, but not all of it. How much you sleep, how much you drink, and what you do after you finish eating also matter. That’s where a walk can help.

The clearest evidence that walking after eating can be beneficial to digestion is seen in its effect on blood sugar. Getting moving right after a meal blunts the post-meal glucose spike better than sitting or exercising before you eat, and the sooner you start, the bigger the effect. Researchers think working muscles soak up sugar from the blood, and since most people sit after dinner, an evening walk may do the most good.

In healthy adults, eating more sugar and refined carbs has been tied to more nighttime stirring and lighter sleep. Among 18-year-olds, days with bigger glucose swings were followed by slightly shorter sleep. Adults who are overweight or those with obesity at risk for type 2 diabetes showed something similar: bigger daytime glucose swings were followed by earlier waking that night, and higher average glucose was tied to less efficient sleep.

Walking’s effects on sleep are promising but modest. A 2026 meta-analysis found that walking lengthened total sleep and cut time spent awake during the night, though it didn’t help people fall asleep faster, and it’s important to note that most trials tested daytime walking. A prevailing pattern was that sessions of 30 minutes or more showed clearer benefits for how well people felt they slept, so a longer walk might be the move.

A review article from the American Heart Association says that exercise is a zeitgeber, a cue that helps set the body clock. According to the review, physical activity generally improves sleep no matter what time of day you do it, and regular moderate-to-vigorous activity can strengthen the body’s daily rhythms.

The one wrinkle is timing. In a study of nearly 15,000 people wearing activity trackers, light or moderate exercise that wrapped up about two hours before bed wasn’t linked to worse sleep. Hard workouts late in the evening were. The easiest way to build in that buffer is to move dinner up. Eating earlier gives you room for the walk and leaves a longer gap before bed, which a large population study linked to better sleep quality.

Time your walk with sunset, and you may get a bonus: the fading light could help cue your body for sleep. As the sun goes down, the light reaching your eyes gets dimmer and less blue. Light-sensing cells in your eyes report that change to your brain’s master clock, which starts preparing to release melatonin and shift you toward sleep.

An after-dinner walk works best when it’s short, easy, and starts soon after you eat. Here are a few ways to get the most from it:

So the next time a food coma hits, lace up instead of lying down. A short, easy walk blunts the post-meal glucose spike, and as a regular habit, it may set you up for a better night’s rest.

Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

#8197. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: Jon and Jess Glassberg / Courtesy COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8196. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A conditions report on the U.S. Forest Service webpage says that a “Huge rock and heavy debris” is currently blocking the trail about a half-mile from the trailhead. One video claims shows an area along Junction Creek Trail near Gudy’s Rest, where a footbridge has been washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a new “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote. “For example, we know that the Colorado Trail along Junction Creek has largely been obliterated and that the trail bridge is gone. In some sections the trail is buried underneath riverflow that was re-routed during the flooding.”

Authorities said that recovery work would likely not begin until spring and summer 2027 due to weather, and discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” another post reads. “Don’t become a statistic — rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”

Another video posted to Instagram shows the sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”

Backpacker reached out to the CDTC for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”

#8193. I Tried the Nike Air Zoom Hyperslide Every Day for a Month and Now I’m Spoiled

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The Hyperice pod hidden in the straps elevates the decadent coddling the Nike Air Zoom Hyperslide delivers. (Photo: 101 Degrees West)

For more than a decade, every morning while I’m hand-grinding coffee beans for my moka pot, I do 15 to 20 squats. It’s a comforting morning routine, but it is mostly a discipline, a way to ensure I don’t let busy days keep me from working on my glutes to counteract hours of sitting.

A month ago, however, I added decadence to my discipline, making me look forward to the coffee-grinding routine (almost) as much as I do the coffee. That decadence comes in the form of a comfy pair of slides and a hot foot massage, bundled together as the Nike x Hyperice Air Zoom Hyperslide.

Is this $250 recovery slide an expensive gimmick? Well . . . yes. But an oh-so-comfortable one that I’m now reluctant to give up.

The slide itself is a slab of supportive foam topped by responsive, low-profile Air Zoom units (the same pressurized-air and trampoline-like tensile-fiber pods used in Nike’s high-end running shoes, here tuned more for comfort than performance). The Air Zoom cushioning feels both plush and lightly bouncy underfoot, and the wide platform provides reassuring stability, making my feet feel coddled and supported while doing my squats, walking around my office, or sitting at my desk.

But that coddling is just the beginning. Hidden beneath the Velcro top straps are a pair of Hyperice pods that magnetically attach to the main instep straps and transmit heat and vibration to the tops of my feet. Buttons on each side of the pods cycle through three levels of vibration (50, 75, and 100 Hz) and three levels of heat (109°F, 113°F, and 117°F). You can also use the Bluetooth-connected phone app, but as far as I can tell, its main benefit is only letting you set the run time longer than the default fifteen minutes.

The first time I used the Hyperslides, I dutifully wore socks and selected the lowest settings, as recommended. Quickly, however, I was cranking them up to high on both heat and vibration. I have, however, kept wearing the socks, because they seem to help wrap my foot and transmit the sensations farther around it rather than having them isolated in one spot on top.

It didn’t take long before I craved the buzzing warmth radiating through my feet each morning, although the sensation felt simply pleasurable, not therapeutic. That was before the day I woke up with a sharp pain between two metatarsal heads that I traced back to a twisting foot plant on a trail run the day before. When I slid my foot into the slide and started the massage, it initially felt a bit intense on the sore spot, but as the heat and vibrations loosened the stiffness, the pain all but disappeared and stayed away all day.

The Hyperslides do what they do better than I ever imagined (having never imagined a heated, vibrating slide), but after using them for a while, I have a couple of nitpicky wishes.

The batteries are supposed to last for an hour on full power, which was pretty close to what I get. Because I almost always restart them after the first fifteen minutes, I run out of juice after two days. They usually sputter out of power before the full 30 minutes on the second day, which I prefer to having them complete the cycle because the dying pods prompt me to plug them in. There’s no battery-level indicator, so if they turn off without dying, I don’t know if I need to charge them unless I remember how many days it’s been since they were charged and how many cycles I’ve run since (I don’t have the mindspace for that). The worst is when I turn them on thinking they are charged, and the battery runs out in a few short minutes—then I have to wait three hours for them to charge. I wish they had some way to let me know how much juice was left.

My only other wish is that I’d like the heat and vibration to reach down to my arch better. But that would require a bigger, more encompassing device, like a boot. Oh! Nike and Hyperice made one of those too. I may have to try them someday, but for now I’ll luxuriate in the easy, slip-on, push-button pleasure that the Hyperslides add to my mornings.

#8192. Calling Washington Backpackers: This $5,000 Grant Could Fund Your PCT Thru-Hike

Walking may be free, but a thru-hike is decidedly expensive: Some Pacific Crest Trail trekkers run up a bill north of $10,000 during a months-long hike. That cost, plus the need to take off work for half a year, presents massive barriers to many would-be thru-hikers.

Seattleite Geoff Burg knows this—and he wants to help. With fellow Washington hikers Keya Gillenwater and Madelyn Scherrer, Burg launched the Pacific Crest Trail Grant in 2025 to award $5,000 to a Washington-based hiker with dreams of completing the trail.

Burg’s connection to the PCT goes back a decade. The attorney was hiking with his kids near Stevens Pass in 2016 when he came across some hikers in distress. Burg volunteered to drive the duo, a pair of PCT thru-hikers in their 60s, into town for medical supplies, then offered them a place to stay in his family’s home. The couple told Burg all about their thru-hike and ultralight philosophy—and the encounter stuck with him.

Over the next several years, Burg chipped away at a section hike of the Washington segment of the PCT. He fell in love with being on the trail, alone or with his kids, and with the greater hiking community around it. Several years later, a conversation with his massage therapist sparked the idea of a scholarship. Well established in his career, and with experience as an advisor for a youth outdoor leadership program, Burg was in a position to help others achieve their long trail dreams.

“We give scholarships for football and baseball and everything else,” he says. “Why not for hiking?”

So he connected with former mentees Gillenwater and Scherrer, a PCT alum, and formed a committee. The grant would offer financial support to a young Washingtonian hoping to complete the long trail.

Burg especially wanted to support young hikers with a financial need; applicants must be between the ages of 18 and 33, with strong ties to Washington state. They should also be able to demonstrate past backpacking experience, which Burg hopes will improve the recipient’s chances of succeeding on a thru-hike and paying the experience forward through volunteer projects like youth outreach or LNT education. Grant recipients who meet that criteria are chosen via a lottery, and must stay in touch with the grant committee during their hikes. Burg emphasizes that the process is not merit-based.

“We already have a community of people that can do this or who want to do this, but within that broader community, there’s so many people that can’t afford it,” he says.

Thirty-two-year-old Seattleite Kayla Provost was the grant’s first recipient. She completed her trek in September 2026, and says she couldn’t have finished the thru-hike without the financial support.

Provost had previously worked as a naturalist guide and, as a Washington resident, felt deeply connected to the Cascades. After losing her mom a few years prior, Provost felt compelled to change her lifestyle. She felt called to the PCT, but financial hurdles posed challenges. After searching “grants for thru-hiking” online, Provost stumbled across a Reddit post about the PCT Grant.

“The grant was truly a lifeline for me,” she says. “Beyond the financial support, the monthly check-ins with the grant committee gave me a sense of accountability and reminded me I had people cheering me on.”

She says the experience redoubled her desire to facilitate outdoor experiences for other people.

“It is incredibly powerful to make a choice, trust yourself enough to follow through, and learn to be comfortable with the uncomfortable,” she says. “The trail offered me a deep sense of confidence, gratitude, and trust in my own ability to navigate the unknown.”

The grant will fund its second thru-hiker in 2027. Through donations, Burg hopes to grow the program into a self-sustaining fund to support more hikers on more trails.

Applications for prospective 2027 PCT thru-hikers are currently open. Washingtonians who meet the criteria can apply by January 31.
