#8129. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Tired of the practically impossible task of packing up the family for a holiday? Here are the best packing cubes for busy families on the go.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

Unleash your little one's love for Lightning McQueen with these top-rated Cars playsets and figures.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!)

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Traveling with kids doesn't;t have to mean getting rid of your entire beauty routine.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Could your child use a little encouragement to read? Disney is here to help with these fabulous books for kids ages 5 to 9.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

#8127. Why Does My Dog Always Steal My Spot? The Reason Will Warm Your Heart

Experts break down the intentions behind your pup’s habit.

Being a dog owner can be extremely rewarding. In many ways, it’s like being given an adorable, cuddly, playful roommate whose main goal in life is to love you unconditionally. I mean, that’s the dream, right? But like with most things, it can also come with a few notable challenges: the main one being their inability to verbally communicate with you. If I had a nickel for every time I wished I knew what my dog was thinking… well… let’s just say I’d be in a different tax bracket by now. It can be frustrating not to know what is going on in those furry heads of theirs, not just in regard to how they’re feeling physically, but on a behavioral level as well. One example that immediately comes to mind is my own dog’s peculiar habit of stealing my spot on the couch as soon as I leave it.

For a little bit of background, my dog’s name is Luna. She is an 8-year-old yellow lab who loves to snore, wag her tail in a helicopter motion, hoard tennis balls and never give them back, and, yes, steal other people’s seats on the furniture. It doesn’t matter if she’s sitting in a similar spot to us, or even right next to us; she will proceed to take your seat the moment you get up to get a snack or use the bathroom or simply grab a nearby blanket. It’s equal parts frustrating and amusing. What exactly is making her do this? As much as I wish my dog could answer that question for me directly (and believe me, I have wondered if she is secretly a human trapped in a dog’s body due to some sort of Beauty and the Beast-style enchantment, but that probably isn’t the case), the habit has inspired me to seek answers elsewhere.

Since I’m sure my dog isn’t the only canine committing furniture theft, Scary Mommy reached out to a few experts to get their insight on what your pup’s real motive may be, and the reason is actually pretty heartwarming.

Right up front: Take comfort in knowing your dog isn’t doing this to upset you. In fact, they love you so much that this is simply an attempt to feel closer to you. “First, your body has warmed the spot, so your dog gets a cozy temperature-controlled bed instantly,” celebrity dog trainer Chrissy Joy shares with Scary Mommy. “Second, your scent is concentrated there, and familiar human scent can be comforting and reassuring to dogs.”

Tracy Murray, dog expert and founder of Saving Fido Dog Walking, echoes this sentiment, explaining that it’s all coming from a place of love. "Warmth is a big part of it,” she admits. “In general, dogs are drawn to heat, and the spot you just left is prime. But it's not just about the warmth, because otherwise they'd be equally drawn to a patch of sun on the floor." Murray adds, "A dog uses their nose like we use our eyes, so the fact that the spot smells like someone they love is awesome. Taking over your place is like sleeping on a pile of your clothes."

And for those of you who worry your furry friend is doing this to establish themselves as the alpha over you, fear not. "The dominance idea has been pretty much debunked,” Murray continues. “With my background in psychology and years working with dogs, what I see is a dog who wants to be close to her person, not one trying to overtake or outrank them."

Just when you thought that little furball couldn’t get any sweeter!

On the other hand, it’s also possible that you yourself have accidentally encouraged this behavior without realizing it. “Another possibility is that stealing your spot has become a learned behavior,” licensed veterinarian Dr. Sarah-Jane Molier explains. “If you react gleefully or offer your dog attention when they jump in your spot, this is a form of ‘positive reinforcement.’ In other words, your dog has learned that stealing your spot gains them positive attention.”

Basically, the main takeaway here is that your dog is just as obsessed with you and you are with them! They want to be wherever you are (or were), and you can’t help but snuggle them for their thievery. So the next time you get up from your comfortable spot on the couch and come back to find it’s been taken over by a hairy, slobbery, wet-nosed seat-stealer, just remember that it’s their way of showing how much they love you.

And, you know what? I guess I can live with that. Luna has already stolen a big piece of my heart. I suppose she might as well have my spot on the couch too.

#8126. How To Get Fantastic Sleep

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

On a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One big one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

Now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you haven’t got around to planting spring-flowering bulbs yet, don’t panic because you can plant all these showstoppers in November. From tiny pastel-hued muscari to alliums the size of softballs, many-petalled tulips to intensely scented hyacinths, the range of bulbs to plant in November is just as exciting as those that need planting in September or October, so don’t feel you’re missing out for a second if you're slow off the starting block this fall.

Growing blooms from bulbs couldn’t be easier, because fall and winter rain will provide all the moisture they need. The secret to getting great results when planting bulbs in November is to sit them on a shallow layer of grit to improve drainage, so creating a drier environment to stop bulb bases rotting in wet winter soil. You could use horticultural grit but poultry grit does exactly the same job and costs a lot less. Just make sure you use a product that’s 100% crushed rock like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart, rather than the type made from oyster shells.

My bulb recommendations will brighten up your garden from February all the way into May and beyond, and return year after year. And I’ve skipped right past the common-or-garden varieties to bring you flowers in standout shades and shapes to create a colorful stir in your yard. Grow these beautiful bulbs in the ground, in raised beds or in pots – but do just grow them! Which of these striking bulbs to plant in late fall will skyrocket your spring garden next year?

November is the very best month to plant tulips. Waiting until temperatures have lowered reduces the risk of fungal disease tulip fire, and cooler temperatures mean bulbs are less likely to rot. Plant tulips in full sun, burying them at a depth that's three times the height of the bulb. Tulips need excellent drainage so dropping a ½-inch layer of grit into the planting holes first is a smart move. If you’re planting tulips in containers then mix a good handful of grit into the potting soil, too.

If it’s a while since you shopped for these spring flowers, you’ll soon find that tulips don’t have to look like tulips anymore! All these show-off varieties are fully hardy in zones 3-8, blooming in April and May when you can expect lots of curious neighbors asking what they are.

Spring-flowering crocus are incredibly hardy so can be planted in November but pick wisely for the best results. Botanical crocus flower early in January or February so have little time to grow roots from a November planting. Crocus vernus, however, blooms February to April, and their bigger bulb-like corms are tougher and store more energy.

While botanical crocus have tiny blooms, the goblet-shaped flowers of Crocus vernus grow to a far more noticeable 5 inches high. And, whether you want to welcome spring into your garden with pristine white petals or drifts of carnival color, there’s a variety to suit. Plant Crocus vernus at a depth that’s equal to three times the corm’s height, in sun or partial shade in zones 4-8, adding ¼ inch of grit to the bottom of each hole, and the bulbs will quickly naturalize. A favorite spot for these crocus is under deciduous trees where bare branches give them the early spring sunshine they need to flower well.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

These little lovelies only grow 18-24 inches tall but they really punch above their height with orchid-like flowers in saturated colors, and florists prize them highly. Dutch iris are better planted in November as any earlier and the bulbs can start sending up their green shoots prematurely, when the tender growth is quickly knobbled by cold weather.

Because these spectacular flowers sit atop a single slender stem, Dutch iris bulbs look better planted in groups, which makes them easier to bury, too. Dig a hole around 6 inches deep in full sun, mix a handful of grit into the soil, and add the bulbs 3 inches apart. In containers, you can pack them more closely at 2 inches apart.

Iris x hollandica bulbs are hardy in zones 5-9, but in zone 5 they benefit from a mulch of shredded leaves thrown over the top to keep them cozy. You can also plant these bulbs in zones 3 and 4 in pots in an unheated greenhouse, ready to move outside when the worst of the winter is over. Dutch iris is a little later to flower than most spring bulbs from May into June, providing a seamless transition into summer.

These ornamental onions are very relaxed when it comes to when they’re planted and, although most folk get their alliums into the ground in October, as long as the soil isn’t frozen solid, they’ll flourish from a November planting. There are dozens of allium varieties with flowers ranging from small pom poms to huge spheres, lasting for up to a month then drying into structural seedheads.

As the size of the bulbs ranges as much as the blooms, use the usual rule of thumb to plant bulbs at a depth equivalent to three times their height. All alliums need full sun, where they’ll thrive in zones 4-9, and be sure to line holes with a layer of grit. While there are alliums that flower in summer, all my recommendations are late spring varieties that bloom from April into June.

There’s one big reason why you should add hyacinths to your garden, and that’s their incredible scent. As the flowerbuds open, their perfume is fresh, reminiscent of cut grass. In full bloom, an intense and intoxicating floral fragrance takes over, warm with vanilla and spicy with clove. Then as the flowers fade, the aroma deepens and becomes more musky. The scent profile can differ by color, too, with purples and blues typically boasting the strongest perfume, while whites and pinks smell a little sweeter, and yellows and oranges spicier.

Emerging in late February, hyacinths add an extra dimension to crisp, cold spring days when their scent hangs in the air. Hardy in zones 4-8, hyacinths prefer to be planted once soil temperatures have dropped, so the bulbs remain dormant but still get the deep chill they need to flower. Choose a sunny spot and plant bulbs at a depth of three times their height, dropping a ½ inch layer of grit into the hole to prevent them rotting. Hyacinths also thrive in a pot, where you can pack bulbs so they’re almost-but-not touching for a fabulous fragrance cloud on a patio or front porch.

Don’t reach for the standard pink, white and blue colors as there are now all sorts of tempting hyacinth tones to choose from.

‘Delft Blue’ does naturalize but gently, and you easily prevent it from travelling far by snipping off faded flower spikes before they set seed. ‘Fantasy Creation’ has sterile flowers so only spreads very slowly through underground division. And Muscari latifolium has a clumping habit so will stay exactly where you put it. All are suitable for zones 4-8 and flower March or April into May.

The more bulbs you buy, the cheaper they get, so if you end up filling your borders with beautiful spring flowers, speed the planting with a labor-saving tool.

The diameter of this bulb planter adjusts to fit different-sized bulbs. It automatically releases soil and is marked with measurements to make getting the correct depth easy.

This long-handled bulb planter with a serrated base is sturdy enough to perform well even in hard ground, and the raised pedal makes it simple to release the excavated soil plug.

Let your drill do all the work with these garden auger bits that fit a standard ⅜” hex shank. The 1.6” bit is perfect for tulips while the 3.5” can handle the biggest allium bulbs.

#8122. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The New York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

Azaleas and rhododendrons paint the spring garden in gorgeous shades of pink, red, orange, and other vibrant colors. But the work of protecting those future flowers starts now. Fall care before winter is essential for keeping these shrubs healthy and ready to bloom abundantly in spring.

Fall azalea care and rhododendron care are all about preparing them for winter dormancy, maintaining healthy roots, and protecting flower buds. Did you know that these shrubs form their buds in summer? Next year’s flowers are already set in buds, so now is the time to preserve and protect them.

Azaleas and rhododendrons are very similar plants with similar care needs in fall. However, keep in mind that there are deciduous and evergreen types with slightly different needs. We’ll point these out here, along with the essential tasks you should be tackling this fall for all your Rhododendron species.

Fall is not the time for heavy annual pruning of rhododendrons or azaleas. Most spring-blooming members of this plant flower on old growth. This means they set buds over the summer. Trimming too hard in the fall will prune away many of the buds that become next spring’s flowers.

The best time for heavy shaping or pruning is right after spring flowering. But this doesn’t mean you can’t or shouldn’t make any cuts in fall. Inspect your shrubs now for dead, damaged, or diseased branches. Remove these using sharp, clean bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8, available on Amazon, which can cut through woody stems up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. For larger branches, switch to loppers or a pruning saw.

Fertilizing late in the season can trigger new growth that only gets damaged in winter conditions. That damage can introduce disease. It’s also a waste of energy that should be going into keeping roots healthy over winter.

Most fertilizing for azaleas and rhododendrons takes place in spring, after flowering. At that time, you can use a product formulated specifically for these shrubs or for any acid-loving shrub. Also, consider the fact that your shrubs might not need feeding at all if they are healthy or thriving.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you suspect your plants need fertilizer, a soil test is the best way to determine their nutrient needs. The MySoil Soil Test Kit measures both soil pH and nutrient levels, helping you identify any deficiencies before deciding whether to feed your shrubs in spring.

You should keep watering your azaleas and rhododendrons right up until the ground freezes, especially if you’re having a dry autumn. Ideally, the ground will be moist before real winter weather sets in. Check the soil regularly using a moisture meter, such as the Yamron 4-in-1, to see whether water is reaching the root zone. Provide a deep soaking as needed, including one as late in the season as possible before the ground freezes.

This matters because many azaleas and rhododendrons are evergreen, making them susceptible to desiccation, or drying out, over winter. Cold, dry winds leech moisture from the leaves, but roots in frozen ground can’t take up any water. This can result in curled, brown leaves and even damaged buds. Ensuring there is moisture in the ground before winter is less important for deciduous types.

Mulch insulates the soil and roots of your flowering shrubs. It helps regulate soil temperature, retains more moisture around the roots, and prevents the root damage caused by soil heaving that occurs during cycles of freezing and thawing.

Organic mulches such as shredded pine bark or partially decomposed, shredded leaves are ideal for mulching azaleas and rhododendrons. If you don't have suitable materials to hand, Garden Pro's shredded pine bark mulch from Home Depot is a good alternative. Layer the mulch around the root zones of shrubs to a depth of 2 to 3 inches (5–8 cm). Keep it a few inches away from stems to prevent trapping moisture that can encourage rot and disease.

Moist soil is important, especially for evergreen shrubs, but too much moisture can also be damaging. Poorly drained soil can lead to root rot and fungal diseases. Eventually, these diseases can kill shrubs.

Look for signs your shrubs are getting waterlogged: standing water around plants, soggy soil long after rainfall, and wilting or yellowing foliage even when the plants have plenty of water. It’s important to try to remediate soggy conditions. You can clear off compacted mulch and other plant debris, divert runoff from other areas, or regrade the surrounding soil, for instance. If the problem isn’t easily fixed, consider relocating the plant in spring.

Evergreen azaleas and rhododendrons add beautiful color and texture to the winter garden, but they are also more vulnerable to winter damage. Winter burn happens when the leaves lose moisture faster than the roots can draw up water to replace it.

Cold and dry winter wind is a primary cause of winter burn on evergreen shrubs, so creating a windbreak can protect them from much of the damage. Set up a barrier on the side of the shrubs that get hit by winter wind, using natural burlap garden fabric, like this from Home Depot, attached to wooden stakes.

Don’t let the barrier actually touch the leaves. They need some airflow to stay healthy. Young shrubs are more likely to need this kind of winter protection. Established shrubs in more sheltered areas are probably fine without it.

Finally, it’s a good idea to look over your shrubs for any signs of problems caused by common azalea pests or diseases. Managing these issues now can prevent them from carrying over into next year’s growing season. Look for stippling or black specks on leaves, which can indicate lace bugs, a common pest of azaleas and rhododendrons. A 10x illuminated magnifying loupe, like this Carson loupe from Amazon, can help you inspect the undersides of leaves, where these tiny insects and their dark droppings are often found.

An unusual number of dying branches, persistent wilting, and many or unusual leaf spots can indicate fungal diseases and root rot. Keep in mind that some spots are normal and that leaf drop is expected in deciduous varieties.

If you do see issues or unusual damage, remove diseased plant material and dispose of it. If issues persist or you don’t know how to identify or treat a particular pest, check with your local extension office for advice.

Fall azalea and rhododendron care isn’t extensive, but it will help you protect next year’s flowers, safeguard vulnerable foliage, and keep roots healthy. Simple steps now help your shrubs enter winter in better condition and improve the chances of a healthy, colorful spring display.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#8120. 17 Books Scary Mommy Editors Absolutely Devoured In October 2026

From new Kingsolver to a Booker-shortlisted Strout!

Some months the book gods really smile down on us, and October was one of those months. What did we read? We thought you'd never ask. We got our hands on Barbara Kingsolver's first novel since Demon Coppherhead, for one. There's a Booker-shortlisted title from Elizabeth Strout that we're dying to discuss more. And we obviously couldn't leave out the new Emily St. John Mandel book already being adapted for TV that, not surprisingly, is every bit as good as everyone says it is. We rounded it out with a historical shipwreck, some radium poisoning, a Grim Reaper romance, and a few old classics particularly well-suited to spooky season. I mean, c'mon... can you really ask for a better spread than that?

Most of the books on this list have already been released, making them TBR-ready. A few won't hit shelves until next spring, but we can confidently say they're 100% worth preordering. Trust, every book on the list has one thing in common: our team couldn't put it down. Here’s everything we couldn't put down and definitely couldn't wait to recommend this month.

The romantasy genre is pretty oversaturated right now, and it can be difficult to find a book that feels truly original. The magic system Dylan has invented feels completely unique. In this world, when your soulmate is born, a golden ring appears around your finger. A red one appears when your sworn enemy, the person who will cause your soulmate's death, is born (or maybe you're born with both already in place). Our main character is a reaper, someone the rich pay to eliminate their sworn enemies for a hefty fee. But what will she do when she gets an assignment that doesn't align with her moral code? — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

Author Andrew Sean Greer describes his latest book as a "charm novel," and it's so fitting for how I felt while reading it. In the novel, we meet our protagonist, who has landed his first real job cataloging items for a Baroness in the Tuscan countryside. While there, he is folded into life at the estate and meets a colorful cast of characters... but he can't quite figure out what's going on around him (and it's not just because of the language barrier). I laughed out loud multiple times during this delightful book, and I'm glad that it will be there for me to reread in the future. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

I won't lie, this book took a bit of pushing through at first. Much like ACOTAR, I assume you're going to have to read the next book or two in the series to fully understand what's happening and why in Book 1. Even though I felt a little clueless for much of it, I love the love and yearning Lee writes here, as well as the atmosphere of the book. I look forward to picking up the next installment and going "ohhhhh" a lot. — Katie McPherson

This book broke me open in the quietest, most devastating way, and I cannot stop thinking about it! Shortlisted for the 2026 Booker Prize and a Barack Obama summer reading pick, it follows Artie Dam, a 57-year-old history teacher in coastal Massachusetts who appears to be living a perfectly decent life while quietly drowning in isolation, and he soon learns a secret he cannot even speak out loud. Strout does what she does better than almost anyone — she takes the ordinary and makes it feel unbearably significant, and the Booker Prize judges called it an example of a new genre they named “radical normalcy,” which is exactly right. It is a short book that will sit with you for a very long time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

Ross is such a beautiful writer, and A Bittersweet Spell is no exception. This book has all the eldritch mystical scene-setting you could ever want; I don't even drink hot tea and I was craving a cup of the stuff every time I read another chapter. The characters feel genuine and fresh (no brooding shadow daddy stereotype here). As always, Ross' magic system is novel and fascinating, and the mystery at the heart of the story unfolds in a very engaging way. Side note: I was literally picturing Brendan Fraser as Lorne and Rachel Weisz as Avalene throughout my read, and honestly, I recommend you do the same. — Katie McPherson

From the author of the epic The Love Songs of W.E.B. Du Bois comes a collection of essays and sketches about what it means to be a Black woman living in America today. I loved the diversity of the writings contained in this book, from freeform poems to deeply researched essays to personal writings about the author's life. This is an incredibly important book from one of our best living authors, and I learned from it as much as I enjoyed its stellar writing. — Sarah Aswell

I am a huge sucker for historical non-fiction about shipwrecks (niche, I know!) and this is one of the best ones I've ever read. David Grann is the GOAT of these types of intricately researched books (Lost City of Z and Killers of the Flower Moon are both excellent), and this is no exception. It follows the very, very doomed journey of the ship The Wager, through the eyes of several of the people aboard, and we get everything that is good about these books: being stranded on an island, getting scurvy, mutiny, and murder. — Sarah Aswell

From the author of Station Eleven comes her most ambitious, mind-bending novel yet. It is 2031; America has fractured, California has declared itself a republic, and for the first time in weeks, the curfew in Los Angeles is lifted. There's a party that everyone gravitates to, but midway through the night the host disappears, guests appear to be in two places at once, and Ari Waker, freshly out of prison after 18 years, is left haunted by the night for years to come. It is already a New York Times bestseller; it is being adapted for television by Mandel herself, and reviewers are calling it the culmination of everything she has ever written. The kind of novel you will be desperate to talk about the second you finish it! — Katie Garrity

Barbara Kingsolver is back with her first book since Demon Copperhead, and it's a good one! This is less epic and more narrow in scope, but no less beautiful. In it, we meet Livia, a rural farmgirl who happens to have an incredibly rare ability to play the piano. She goes to college against her mother's wishes, only to have her life altered in unimaginable ways. This book is about the big things: life, love, and art, and it is very, very moving. It also has a playlist of piano pieces that go along with the book — so fun! — Sarah Aswell

B.K. Borison is a NYT bestselling author who simply does not miss, and Grim Tidings is already being called her best book yet. Darcy Moore is a Grim Reaper who is absolutely done with death, so she decides to save her next assignment instead of collecting him, which puts her directly in the path of Gabriel, a skeptical Guardian Angel protecting his little corner of the world as his wings depend on it. It is a grumpy-x-grumpy enemies-to-lovers romance with Halloween vibes and real emotional depth — reviewers are reporting full-on crying on public transportation, which is always the highest possible endorsement. If you loved Good Spirits, you will absolutely devour Grim Tidings! — Katie Garrity

This book has a Young Readers Edition, and it's a great option to read along with your middle-grade kid! My daughter and I devoured our copies and had so much fun talking about it together, even though the story is sad and shocking. This is a non-fiction book about the young women who worked in factories during the early 1900s, painting radium onto watch faces and airplane equipment. A huge number of them got radium poisoning — and many lawsuits followed. This book is about workers' rights and women's rights, but it's also about survival and perseverance. — Sarah Aswell

I just got back from Salem, where I toured the actual House of the Seven Gables... and I spent most of the tour wishing I’d finished the book beforehand! So I made it a point to remedy that immediately. Hawthorne’s 1851 novel is about a family slowly rotting under an ancestral curse, which is all the more fascinating when you consider that his own great-great-grandfather was a judge in the Salem witch trials who never repented (Hawthorne’s cousin, Susannah Ingersoll, was one of the house's owners). Fair warning: The prose here is very 1851 and takes some patience, but the history underneath it is worth it. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

After I heard Ann Patchett's glowing review of this book, I had to pick it up, and let's just say she was right. This book is about a young man in the far reaches of Scotland (an isolated island, to be exact) who leaves his life of sheep-raising and weaving to go to fashion/textile school. When he returns to care for a sick grandmother, he clashes with his dad about his lifestyle... but that's only the beginning! I know this lovely and difficult book will be in my top 5 reads for 2026. — Sarah Aswell

I picked up this box set because I wanted to re-read Carrie before Mike Flanagan’s new Prime Video series, then realized I’d somehow never read The Shining or Salem’s Lot... the first of which I have extra motivation for since I stayed at The Stanley, aka the hotel that inspired it, last year (clearly have a thing for reading books about places I visit!). All three are just classic early Stephen King and the set is beautifully designed, making this an easy gift for the horror person in your life. — Julie Sprankles

Jon Klassen is a Caldecott Medal winner who has absolutely never missed, and Abner and the Bubblegum Balloon is already generating serious buzz as one of the most anticipated picture books of the season. It has that signature Klassen deadpan humor, sparse text, and perfectly timed visual comedy that makes his books just as hilarious for the adults reading aloud as for the kids listening. If you have a child in your life who loved I Want My Hat Back or This Is Not My Hat, this is an immediate add to cart. The picture book that earns a permanent spot on the shelf and gets requested at bedtime on repeat! — Katie Garrity

#8119. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”

Finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

#8118. Why Do I Get Dizzy When I Stand Up? Experts Say No, This Isn't Normal

“If something is repeatedly interfering with how you feel or function, you deserve a thoughtful evaluation.”

It happens when you get up from your desk at work, from playing on the floor with your kids, even when you get out of bed first thing in the morning. Lately, whenever you go from lying or sitting to standing, you get a little dizzy. You have to pause and close your eyes, maybe grab onto something solid, and wait a few seconds before taking off. So what gives? Why do you get dizzy when you stand up now, and is it normal?

Well, medical experts agree that getting dizzy every time you stand up is categorically not normal, and it’s worth making an appointment with your doctor to investigate why it happens to you. They say the answer is likely something easy to fix, and anything impacting your daily functioning is worth the investigation.

Adjusting your blood flow to your current activity level is one of those things our brain does all on its own that we don’t really appreciate fully until it goes wrong.

“When someone stands up, gravity pulls blood toward the lower half of the body, and the nervous system has to respond quickly to maintain blood flow to the brain. If that adjustment doesn’t happen efficiently, you can feel lightheaded, see spots, or feel as though you’re about to faint,” says Dr. Motisola Lewis, MD, internal medicine physician and founder of Lewis Medical NY.

For women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, dizziness upon standing can be a symptom of many different things.

“Some of the most common causes are dehydration, not eating or drinking enough, low blood pressure, anemia, blood loss, and medication side effects. In women in their 30s through 50s, I also think about heavy menstrual bleeding, hormonal transitions, and medications that can affect blood pressure or heart rate. Sometimes there is more than one contributing factor,” Lewis explains.

It’s also important to distinguish between dizziness and vertigo so you can accurately describe your experience to your doctor.

“If they feel lightheaded, faint, or like they might pass out, I would think about blood pressure issues, especially orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure with standing. Dehydration, medication side effects or interactions, blood sugar fluctuations, cardiovascular issues, and other medical conditions can also cause lightheadedness,” says Dr. Kim Bell, a doctor of physical therapy who specializes in dizziness, vertigo, balance problems, and fall prevention.

“If they describe more of a brief spinning sensation when they get up, I would also want to rule out benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV, which is the most common inner ear cause of vertigo. BPPV can cause momentary dizziness or spinning with position changes such as sitting up in bed or getting out of bed.”

If you’ve made an appointment with your doctor to discuss your dizziness, ask yourself a few questions and log the answers for a week or two before you go. Pay attention to what the dizziness feels like, what movement or position triggers it, and how long it lasts, Bell says. “Those details can provide important clues about the cause.”

If it happens once, OK, maybe you were just dehydrated. But if it happens frequently, no, that’s not normal at all, Lewis and Bell agree.

“I would not want someone to assume that their height, age, stress level, or tendency to ‘stand up too fast’ explains recurring dizziness without actually investigating the cause,” says Bell.

If you’ve ever had a doctor chalk up your dizziness to standing up too fast, anxiety, or literally just being too tall (this really happens), look for a second opinion.

“Women deserve to be heard before their symptoms are explained away. Many women are exceptionally good at pushing through discomfort. They get the children ready, go to work, care for their families, and carry on even when they don’t feel well. Sometimes they normalize their symptoms because they’ve been told that what they’re experiencing is just stress, aging, or something they have to live with. But if you're consistently dizzy when you stand, exhausted despite sleeping, experiencing a racing heart, or struggling to function the way you used to, it’s worth asking why,” says Lewis.

This doesn’t mean your dizziness is pointing to a rare or serious condition; usually the cause is something simple and totally treatable, Lewis adds.

If you’re experiencing certain symptoms along with dizziness, it warrants a more urgent assessment, Lewis says. Here are the symptoms that Bell and Lewis say would make them want to see you ASAP:

If you experience new neurological symptoms, including sudden weakness or numbness on one side, confusion, double vision, difficulty speaking, or a sudden severe headache, that’s your sign to head to your nearest emergency room, Lewis notes.

If you’ve heard about POTS lately, well, that’s because it’s becoming a lot more common.

All around the world, studies show health experts are diagnosing more people than ever before with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS: an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes your heart to beat faster than normal when you go from sitting or lying down to standing up. Unsurprisingly, dizziness upon standing is one of its hallmark symptoms. The condition can be caused by severe viral infections; public health experts believe the COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive number of previously healthy people to develop POTS.

While it might be in the zeitgeist right now, Lewis says POTS is not the most common explanation for dizziness upon standing. Women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s can have so much happening in their bodies that the dizziness may be the result of more than one factor as well — think sleep disruptions, hormonal changes, and iron deficiency.

If anything in your life, like getting dizzy when you stand, is interfering with how you feel or function, “you deserve a thoughtful evaluation” from your healthcare provider, Lewis says.

#8117. When can a kid ride in the front seat?

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

Has your big kid started asking – or downright begging – to graduate to the front seat of the car finally? Most kids start pining for the coveted spot long before they are big enough to safely sit up front.

Of course,safetyis your number one concern, butas their endless pleas wear you down, you might be wondering:when can I let them sit up front? Is it really that big of a deal to keep them in the back? We’ve been there. For help, we reached out to childhood safety experts to understand why the AAP recommends waiting until at least the age of 13 before letting your child ride in the front seat.

While the AAP guidelines are clear, local and federal laws (or, rather, lack thereof) muddy the waters. Lia Tuso, a Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST) based in Buffalo, New York, tells Moms.com, “Unfortunately, when it comes to child passenger safety, the laws are the bare minimum.” There are no federal laws in the U.S. prohibiting children from riding in the front seat, but there are a handful of state laws. Delaware, for example, requires children to be at least 12 years old and 65 inches tall to sit in the front seat, while California mandates that children must be eight years old and over 57 inches tall. And it’s not just the U.S. – other peer nations’ laws are surprisingly lax around the topic. Most state laws in Australia, for example, require children to be at least seven years old to ride shotgun.

Tuso does not mince words about why younger children in the front seat of a car is so dangerous, saying, “The frontal airbags are designed to protect adult male bodies, not pre-pubescent children. The frontal airbags deploy at about 200 mph and they are designed to make contact with the average-sized male adult's bones. They simply aren't designed to protect children who don't have the same bone strength as an adult.”

While predicting your pre-teen son's future height isn't an exact science there are ways to see if he's above or below the average height of his peers

Corri Miller-Hobbs, a safety expert with the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU, agrees. She also oversees the Virginia chapter Safe Kids Worldwide and tells Moms.com, “[Keeping children under 13 in the back seat] places the child in a seating position that is further away from a frontal crash, the most common type of crash.”

Tuso points out that research performed by the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia shows that children who are exposed to frontal airbags are twice as likely to suffer injury than children riding in the back seat. “The injuries that are most frequently seen from children riding in the front seat are head injuries such as traumatic brain injury and superficial head trauma, thoracic/chest injuries, abdominal injuries, pelvic injuries, and orthopedic injuries such as long bone fractures,” Dr. Alexis Javier, a Pediatrician with Memorial Hermann Health System in Houston, Texas, tells Moms.com. Importantly, Miller-Hobbs adds, “Injuries vary and can depend on how close the child is sitting to the frontal airbag and whether they were correctly restrained with a child restraint or safety belt.”

Tuso recommends seeking guidance from Child Passenger Safety Technician for every car seat transition, saying that too often, “parents will schedule a car seat installation check with a CPST for their newborn, but don't finish the journey to the front seat.”

“Oftentimes we see kids sitting upfront, who should still not only be in the back seat, but also in a booster!” Tuso says, “Most children will need a booster until ten to 12 years old. So parents should first ask, has the child maxed out the height/weight limits on their current booster seat?”

In addition to being physically developed enough to be safe in the front seat, Tuso shares important guidelines to ensure the correct fit for an adult seatbelt on a child, called the Five-Step Test.

“Even if your child passes the seat belt fit test in one seating position in one vehicle, that doesn’t mean they will pass the test in all vehicles and seating positions… so be sure to perform the seat belt fit test in any vehicle and any seating position your child may utilize,” Miller-Hobbs says. She also advises moving the passenger seat as far back from the airbag as possible for your child.

“Be sure to consider your child’s developmental level and personality when explaining the rationale,” Miller-Hobbs says, “Avoid using scary details about injuries versus talking about making healthy and safe choices, as with other aspects of their life.” She offers a few ideas to help make the backseat more appealing, such as:

Adventures have never been more fun, or easy, with one of these 8 travel essentials.

Tuso adds that watching crash test videos together on YouTube can be an effective way to demonstrate the necessity for strict rules around riding up front. “There is a lot of peer pressure around this age, especially with school drop-offs, but reminding your child of the importance of riding safely will set them up for success... even when they're driving on their own!” she says.

“We understand caregivers and children are excited and proud when new milestones are achieved,” Miller-Hobbs adds, “However, moving out of a car seat or belt positioning booster seat into a seat belt system should not be a milestone that is rushed.” Tuso agrees, saying, “The safest place for children under 13 is the back seat. While growing up is inevitable, injuries are preventable... there's no rush to the front seat.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is when a lot of homeowners get around to overseeding cool-season lawns. You rake out the thin spots, spread the seed and set the sprinkler going. Two weeks later, plenty of those patches still look like bare dirt, and it's tempting to blame the seed.

Chances are, the seed is fine. Anyone who has spent time seeding a lawn knows some grasses are just slow, and a couple of the usual fall picks can take weeks to show anything. Fall is still a smart time to seed, though. The ground stays warm from summer while the air cools off, and the rain usually picks back up.

Grab the bag and check what's in it. A blend might mix ryegrass, fescue and bluegrass, and those don't keep the same schedule. Ryegrass can be up in about a week, while bluegrass may take a month, so a new blend looks spotty at first. And green doesn't mean done – new grass still needs several more weeks to root in.

The rest happens underground. Cool-season seed generally won't germinate until the soil is above about 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and colder ground can leave it sitting there until spring. Push a soil thermometer (like this one from the Urban Worm Store) in to see where yours is. The seed also has to stay damp and reach dirt, not just rest on dead thatch.

Any lawn that slows down and browns a little in July, then greens back up when the nights cool off, is a cool-season lawn. Bermuda, zoysia and bahiagrass are the opposite; those warm-season grasses do better seeded in late spring or early summer, after the soil has warmed up.

Across the upper Midwest and other northern areas, the ground cools early, so the window runs from mid-August to mid-September and has usually closed by October. Farther south, in places like Tennessee, there's room to seed into mid-October. Anything sown late has less time to get established before the first hard freeze.

Perennial ryegrass is what you want when a bare spot has to look green before winter – a worn strip by the mailbox, let's say, or the patch where the dog cuts across the yard. It's often up in 5 to 10 days. Sow it early in the fall window. One option is Pennington Fairway Supreme perennial ryegrass from Lowe's, which comes in a 50-pound bag with fertilizer mixed in. It's at its best in cool, moist weather and doesn't take drought well. In the South, it mostly gets sown over dormant Bermuda for winter color, not as a permanent lawn.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your USDA Planting Zone is somewhere between Kansas and the Carolinas, your lawn may well be tall fescue already. Bluegrass struggles in those hot summers, but fescue's deep roots carry it through dry spells. Seed usually comes up within a week or two. GreenView turf-type tall fescue seed, available on Amazon, comes in 7-pound bags. Fescue grows in clumps rather than spreading, though, so thin spots won't fill in by themselves and need reseeding in early to mid-fall.

Bluegrass asks for patience up front. It usually takes at least two weeks to sprout and can take closer to a month. Once it's up, it spreads by underground rhizomes into a thick, soft lawn that can fill worn spots back in. It does best where summers stay fairly cool. Get it down right at the start of your fall window. Home Depot stocks a 5.6-pound bag of Scotts Turf Builder Kentucky bluegrass mix.

Keen for your grass to get a move on? Look this way...

Get down and look closely at a patch that still hasn't come up. You'll often find the seed sitting on top of old thatch or dead leaves instead of on the soil. It dries out between waterings up there; indeed, its first root may never reach the soil. Before you seed, mow the grass you already have down to about 1 1/2 to 2 inches (4–5cm), rake out the loose debris, then scratch up the surface until you can see bare, crumbly soil.

On small areas, a stiff 16-tine steel bow rake like the one Walmart carries will break up a crusted surface. Once the seed is down, rake over it lightly to work it into the top 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3–6mm) of soil, or press it in with the back of the rake. Don't worry if some seed is still showing, since bluegrass actually sprouts better with a little light.

On a breezy afternoon, soil watered at breakfast can be pale and crusty by the evening. Seed that's begun to swell can dry out and fail. Short, light sprinkles once or twice a day, and one more on days like that, keep the top inch (2.5cm) damp, not muddy. Long soaks can float seed into low spots or waterlog the soil, and an overnight rain counts as a turn.

A pulsing impact head can knock seed loose, but an oscillating sprinkler lays water down in a soft sweep. With the Melnor XT turbo oscillating sprinkler from Amazon, you can narrow the spray so it stays on the seed, not the sidewalk. For days when nobody's home, the Orbit single-outlet hose faucet timer from Home Depot can run short cycles as often as once an hour. Once seedlings have roots, water less often but more deeply.

A thin layer of screened compost over the seed helps keep the surface from drying out so fast. That layer gives the seed some protection from heavy rain, too. Spread it no more than about 1/4 inch (6mm) deep. You should still be able to see a little seed and soil through it.

Thicker isn't better. Grass seed carries only a small store of energy, and seed buried too deep can use it up before the shoot reaches light —, and fine bluegrass seed may not sprout under a heavy layer at all.

If you don't have finished compost, a bag of Scotts Turf Builder lawn soil from Home Depot is made for overseeding and top dressing.

So how long should you wait? With ryegrass or tall fescue in soil that's stayed warm and damp, about three weeks is a fair wait. Before reseeding, scrape back a little soil and look. Swollen or split seed is still working, while seed that looks dry and unchanged probably dried out or never touched the soil. Old seed can be the culprit too, so check the packaging date.

Don't count on starter fertilizer to hurry any of this along. Seed carries its own food for germination, and starter fertilizer is there to feed seedlings once roots form – too much can burn tender new grass. If your fall window has closed, it's better to stop than to keep sowing into cold soil. Some people dormant seed instead, spreading it in late fall once the soil is too cold for sprouting but before the ground freezes. Otherwise, early next fall is the more reliable time to try again.

Slow grass seed usually just needs a few more weeks. Choose the right grass for your area, sow it while the soil is still warm, and keep it damp. That will do more than any quick fix. With some patience, those bare spots may be filled in by the time you mow next spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
